title: Neural networks
section: You already own a neural network
text:
You already own a neural network




Logistic regression:
\[p = \sigma(w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_p x_p + b), \qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\]
A neuron (unit): weighted sum → bias → non-linear activation. \(w\) = weights, \(b\) = bias.
That is the whole building block. Everything else is wiring.
Its limit is geometric: \(p \ge 0.5 \iff z \ge 0\), and \(z = 0\) is a straight line (a hyperplane). One neuron draws one straight boundary.

title: Neural networks
section: Why one neuron is not enough
text:
Why one neuron is not enough






XOR and the two rings: no \(w_1, w_2, b\) separate them. Logistic regression scores 55 %.
Minsky & Papert (1969) made this point and the field stalled for fifteen years.
The fix was obvious and un-trainable until backpropagation: let several neurons each draw a soft line, then let one more neuron combine the lines.

title: Neural networks
text:
The multilayer perceptron




One hidden layer of \(H\) units, one output, one person \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^p\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{z}^{(1)} &= \mathbf{W}^{(1)\top}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)} \\
\mathbf{a}^{(1)} &= g(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}) \\
z^{(2)} &= \mathbf{W}^{(2)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)} \\
p &= \sigma(z^{(2)})
\end{aligned}\]
\(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\): \(p\times H\); \(\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\): \(H\) numbers. For \(n\) people, stack \(\mathbf{x}\) as rows of \(\mathbf{X}\) and it is all matrix multiplication → GPUs → five lines of R.
Parameters: \(pH + 2H + 1\). For us (\(p\approx45\), \(H=30\)): 1,411.

title: Neural networks
section: “Deep” just means more of the same
text:
“Deep” just means more of the same
\[\mathbf{a}^{(2)} = g\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(2)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}\right), \qquad
\mathbf{a}^{(3)} = g\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(3)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(2)} + \mathbf{b}^{(3)}\right), \ \dots\]





Each layer re-describes the previous one’s output. Depth lets a network compose simple features into complex ones with far fewer units than one very wide layer would need (edges → textures → parts → objects).

text:
Activation functions: the non-linearity is the point















Formula
Derivative
Use

\(1/(1+e^{-z})\)

Without a non-linear \(g\), layers collapse: a product of matrices is a matrix → one linear model. The squash is what lets eight neurons make a ring.
Saturation: where sigmoid/tanh are flat, the derivative ≈ 0, so earlier layers stop learning — the vanishing gradient. ReLU’s derivative is exactly 1 on the positive side; that is most of why 2012 happened.

title: Neural networks
text:
The loss: what “wrong” means
\[L = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\Big[y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\Big]\]

Binary cross-entropy = the negative log-likelihood logistic regression maximises. Nothing new.
Punishes confident wrong answers brutally: \(p=0.99\) when \(y=0\) costs 4.6; \(p=0.6\) costs 0.9.
Smooth → has a gradient everywhere. Accuracy has no useful gradient, so nothing is trained on it directly.
Regression: MSE. Multi-class: categorical cross-entropy. Survival/ordinal/custom: write your own.

For the worked example: \(L = -\log(0.5973) = 0.5154\).

title: Neural networks
text:
Gradient descent: walk downhill





\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta} \qquad \text{for every weight and bias}\]

Start with small random weights. 2. Compute the loss and its gradient (direction of steepest increase).
Step against it, by the learning rate η. 4. Repeat for many epochs.

Same knob, same trade-off as XGBoost’s learn_rate this morning.

title: Neural networks
section: Backpropagation is the chain rule — step 1: the output
text:
Backpropagation is the chain rule — step 1: the output
We need \(\partial L/\partial\theta\) for every weight. One backward sweep, reusing each layer’s result.
Output layer. Sigmoid + cross-entropy gives a small miracle: \[\delta^{(2)} \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}} = p - y\] How wrong, with a sign. Example: \(\delta^{(2)} = 0.5973 - 1 = \mathbf{-0.4027}\).
Then, since \(z^{(2)} = \sum_h W^{(2)}_h a^{(1)}_h + b^{(2)}\): \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(2)}_h} = \delta^{(2)} a^{(1)}_h, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)}\]
Example: \(\partial L/\partial\mathbf{W}^{(2)} = -0.4027\times(0.6044,\ 0.1974) = (-0.2434,\ -0.0795)\).

title: Neural networks
section: Step 2: pass the blame back through the hidden layer
text:
Step 2: pass the blame back through the hidden layer
How much did each hidden activation contribute to the error? \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(1)}_h} = \delta^{(2)}\,W^{(2)}_h \;\Rightarrow\; (-0.4027)(0.7,\ -0.4) = (-0.2819,\ 0.1611)\]
Through the activation (\(a = \tanh z\), so multiply by \(1 - a^2\)): \[\delta^{(1)}_h = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(1)}_h}\,(1-(a^{(1)}_h)^2) \;\Rightarrow\; (-0.2819)(0.6347),\ (0.1611)(0.9610) = (-0.1789,\ 0.1548)\]
Input weights (\(z^{(1)}_h = \sum_j W^{(1)}_{jh}x_j + b^{(1)}_h\)): \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}_{jh}} = \delta^{(1)}_h\,x_j \;\Rightarrow\;
\begin{pmatrix}1.0\\0.5\end{pmatrix}(-0.1789,\ 0.1548) = \begin{pmatrix}-0.1789 & 0.1548\\ -0.0895 & 0.0774\end{pmatrix}\]

title: Neural networks
text:
Step 3: one gradient-descent step, η = 0.5
\[\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \to \begin{pmatrix}0.5895 & -0.3774\\ 0.2447 & 0.7613\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathbf{b}^{(1)} \to (0.1895,\ 0.0226),\quad
\mathbf{W}^{(2)} \to (0.8217,\ -0.3603),\quad b^{(2)} \to 0.2514\]
Forward pass again with the new weights: \(\mathbf{p = 0.6966}\), loss \(0.3615\) (was 0.5154).

The network moved toward the right answer for this person. Average the gradients over all \(n\) people, repeat a few thousand times, and it has learned. That is all learning means here: the numbers in \(\mathbf{W}\) changed.

Frameworks (torch, TensorFlow, JAX) derive the backward pass for any architecture automatically — automatic differentiation. You write the forward pass. The maths does not change.

title: Neural networks
section: The same thing, in matrix form (Tutorial 7 Part B)
text:
The same thing, in matrix form (Tutorial 7 Part B)

fw  <- forward(X, W1, b1, W2, b2); P <- fw$P; A1 <- fw$A1
dZ2 <- (P - y) / n                   # delta at the output          (n x 1)
dW2 <- t(A1) %*% dZ2                 # blame for hidden->output weights   (H x 1)
dA1 <- dZ2 %*% t(W2)                 # pass the blame back through W2     (n x H)
dZ1 <- dA1 * (1 - A1^2)              # through the tanh                   (n x H)
dW1 <- t(X) %*% dZ1                  # blame for input->hidden weights    (p x H)
W1 <- W1 - lr * dW1;  b1 <- b1 - lr * colSums(dZ1)
W2 <- W2 - lr * dW2;  b2 <- b2 - lr * sum(dZ2)

Five lines of backpropagation, two of gradient descent. Run 500 times → the ring.

title: Neural networks
text:
Making training work

Initialisation: small random weights, never all zero (identical units would get identical gradients and never differentiate). Xavier/Glorot (tanh) and He (ReLU) scale the randomness to the fan-in. Different seeds → slightly different networks; report it.
Vanishing / exploding gradients: each backward step multiplies by a weight and an activation derivative; products of many small numbers → 0, of large ones → ∞. Fixes: ReLU, good init, gradient clipping, batch normalisation, residual connections.
Scale the inputs: gradient descent on hh_income in ringgit and age in years spends all its steps on income. step_normalize() — not optional.

text:
Networks overfit by default
1,411 weights on ~3,200 people per fold — about 2 people per parameter; a classical statistician wants 10–20 events per parameter. Left alone, training loss → 0, validation AUC falls, probabilities pile up at 0 and 1.

title: Neural networks
text:
Architecture choices for tabular data

Width: 8–64 units for a few thousand rows. Depth: one hidden layer is usually enough; two (32 → 16) occasionally helps; more rarely does.
Activation: ReLU for depth; tanh/sigmoid fine for one small layer.
Output: parsnip sets it from set_mode() — sigmoid/softmax/identity.
What to tune, in order: learning rate (if not L-BFGS) → width → decay/dropout → epochs (early stopping) → batch size → depth.

Universal approximation says a wide-enough single layer can represent any continuous function. It does not say gradient descent will find it, or that 3,200 people will identify it. Depth gets there with far fewer parameters.

title: Neural networks
section: Convolution, recurrence, attention — one slide each
text:
Convolution, recurrence, attention — one slide each


CNN — a 3×3 filter slides across the image and fires where it matches a pattern; layers of filters build edges → textures → parts → objects; pooling shrinks and adds translation invariance. Transfer learning: start from a net trained on millions of natural images, retrain the last layers on your 2,000 fundus photos.

RNN / LSTM — process a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state (memory); LSTM gates decide what to keep and forget. ECG, vital-sign streams, early EHR-sequence models. Largely superseded by …

Transformer — every position looks at every other and learns where to look (attention); no recurrence, massively parallel. The basis of BERT/GPT, modern vision models, and the medical foundation models now arriving.

title: Neural networks
section: How deep learning fails in health
text:
How deep learning fails in health

Shortcut learning: pneumonia classifiers that read the portable-X-ray marker; skin-cancer models that detect the dermatologist’s ruler; COVID CXR models that learned the hospital (DeGrave et al. 2021).
Dataset shift: a new scanner, population or protocol — performance collapses silently.
Over-confidence: badly calibrated out of the box (Guo et al. 2017) → temperature scaling / Platt before deployment.
Data and label hunger; label noise propagates.
Reproducibility: seeds, GPU non-determinism, undocumented pre-processing.
Equity: under-performance on under-represented groups unless measured.

Same medicine as the rest of the workshop: leak-free splits by patient, honest resampling, calibration, subgroup checks, explanations used as audits.

section: This morning’s bake-off, this hour’s question
text:
This morning’s bake-off, this hour’s question
This morning you ranked four model families on five folds. Two questions were left hanging:

How much should we trust a number like “AUC 0.853”? (Resampling.)
Every model was run on guessed settings. What are the right ones? (Tuning.)

Both answers come from the same tool: fitting the model many times on data it has not seen.

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
The same model, 25 random splits

many_splits <- mc_cv(dm_data, prop = 0.80, times = 25, strata = undx_dm)
lr_many     <- fit_resamples(lr_wf, many_splits, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
collect_metrics(lr_many, summarize = FALSE) |> ggplot(aes(.estimate)) + geom_histogram(bins = 12)


Nothing changed except which 1,000 people were held out. Test AUC ranges from ~0.80 to ~0.88.
Any single number in that range is a legitimate “test-set AUC”. A paper that reports 0.88 is not lying — it is reporting one draw from a distribution and calling it the answer.
With ~115 cases in a test set, that spread is unavoidable. Smaller test sets are worse.


Report mean ± standard error across resamples. collect_metrics() gives you both. The SE is the number that tells you whether two models actually differ.

folds keep class balance
always, for outcomes under ~30 %


Monte-Carlo CV
mc_cv(times = 25)
repeated random splits
quick variance check


Bootstrap
bootstraps(times = 25)
sample with replacement; OOB = assessment
small n; confidence intervals (int_pctl())


Leave-one-out
loo_cv()
n folds
tiny n; high variance; rarely worth it


Grouped
group_vfold_cv(group = patient_id)
whole clusters held out together
repeated measures, multi-site


Rolling origin
sliding_period(), rolling_origin()
train on past, assess on future
time series, forecasting


Validation set
initial_validation_split()
one fixed assessment set
n in the millions; deep learning


Nested CV
outer vfold_cv + inner tuning
tune inside each outer fold
unbiased estimate of a tuned pipeline (see later)

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
k-fold, pictured





Five or ten? 10-fold has less bias (90 % of data per fit); 5-fold is twice as fast and fine for tuning big grids. We use 5 in the workshop for time; use 10 (repeated) in your paper.

Jian et al. (2022)

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
What happens inside one fold

dm_folds$splits[[1]]
analysis(dm_folds$splits[[1]])      # 4/5 of the training set: recipe is prepped HERE, model fitted HERE
assessment(dm_folds$splits[[1]])    # 1/5: baked with the analysis set's medians/SDs, scored


Imputation medians, scaling, dummy levels, SMOTE, feature selection — everything estimated from data is estimated on the analysis set only, five separate times.
This is why pre-processing lives in a recipe inside a workflow and not in a mutate() before the split. A mutate() that uses the whole data set has already leaked.
The same discipline applies to variable selection: selecting predictors on the full data and then cross-validating the model is the classic way to get an optimistic AUC (Ambroise & McLachlan 2002).

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Parameters vs hyperparameters

Parameters are learned from data by fit(): regression coefficients, split points, network weights.
Hyperparameters are set before fitting and control how flexible the model may be: mtry, min_n, tree_depth, learn_rate, penalty, cost, rbf_sigma, neighbors, hidden_units, epochs.

Each hyperparameter is a position on the bias–variance curve. Tuning = finding the sweet spot empirically, on resamples.

boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune(), sample_size = tune())

tune() is a placeholder. The workflow still works; it just cannot be fit() until the placeholders are filled.

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Grid search





For each candidate setting → k-fold CV → average metric. Pick the best. Cost = candidates × folds model fits.

Jian et al. (2022)

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Defining the search space: dials

xgb_params <- extract_parameter_set_dials(xgb_tune_wf) |>
  update(
    learn_rate  = learn_rate(range = c(-2.5, -0.5)),   # log10 scale: 0.003 .. 0.32
    tree_depth  = tree_depth(range = c(2L, 8L)),
    min_n       = min_n(range = c(5L, 60L)),
    sample_size = sample_prop(range = c(0.5, 1))
  )


Every tunable argument has a dials object with a default range and, where sensible, a log transform (learn_rate, penalty, cost, rbf_sigma, loss_reduction). Tune those on the log scale or you waste 90 % of the grid on one end.
Defaults are deliberately wide. Narrow them with domain sense — a learning rate of 10⁻¹⁰ is not a candidate.
Ranges that depend on the data (mtry ≤ number of predictors) need finalize(mtry(), x = baked_predictors) or an explicit update().

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Regular vs space-filling grids






grid_regular(xgb_params, levels = 3)              # 3^4 = 81 candidates, 3 distinct values each
grid_space_filling(xgb_params, size = 20)         # 20 candidates, 20 distinct values each

With 4+ parameters, a regular grid explodes and still only tries a few values per parameter. Space-filling (Latin hypercube / max-entropy) spreads a fixed budget evenly. tune_grid(grid = 20) builds one for you.

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Smarter than a grid









Strategy
Function
Idea
When




Random search
grid_random()
sample candidates at random
cheap, surprisingly good


Racing
finetune::tune_race_anova()
after a few folds, drop candidates that are already significantly worse
default choice: same answer as a full grid at a fraction of the cost


Bayesian optimisation
tune_bayes()
fit a model of metric ~ hyperparameters, propose the next most promising candidate
expensive models, few evaluations


Simulated annealing
finetune::tune_sim_anneal()
local random walk that sometimes accepts worse moves
refining around a good region




xgb_race <- tune_race_anova(xgb_tune_wf, resamples = dm_folds, param_info = xgb_params, grid = 30,
                            metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class),
                            control = control_race(verbose_elim = TRUE))
plot_race(xgb_race)

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Reading the results

collect_metrics(xgb_tuned)                  # mean, n, std_err for every candidate x metric
autoplot(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc")     # one panel per parameter: flat = doesn't matter; slope/peak = does
show_best(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)

Two ways to pick:

select_best(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc")                                    # the numerically best
select_by_one_std_err(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc", tree_depth, desc(min_n))  # the SIMPLEST within 1 SE of best


The one-standard-error rule (Breiman 1984): among candidates whose score is within one SE of the best, choose the simplest. Simpler = less overfit, faster, easier to explain, and the “best” was probably best by luck anyway.


Remind: metric = must be named in tune ≥ 2.0. The sorting arguments of select_by_one_std_err define “simpler”: smaller tree_depth, larger min_n.

title: Resampling and tuning
section: Finalise, then — and only then — the test set
text:
Finalise, then — and only then — the test set

xgb_final_wf <- finalize_workflow(xgb_tune_wf, select_best(xgb_race, metric = "roc_auc"))
xgb_last     <- last_fit(xgb_final_wf, split = dm_split, metrics = cls_metrics)

collect_metrics(xgb_last)          # test-set metrics, one shot
collect_predictions(xgb_last)      # test-set predictions, for curves and thresholds
extract_workflow(xgb_last)         # the fitted workflow: save it, deploy it


last_fit() fits on all training data and predicts the test set in one call. It is the only function in the workshop that touches dm_test.
If CV says 0.86 and the test says 0.80, something is wrong (leak in CV, distribution shift, bad luck with 115 cases). Investigate; do not re-tune on the test set.

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Parallel processing (it changed)

library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1)   # that's it; tune/fit_resamples pick it up


tune ≥ 1.3 uses the future (or mirai) framework. doParallel::registerDoParallel() from older tutorials does nothing now.
Each worker needs memory for a copy of the data; on an 8 GB laptop stop at 3–4 workers.
ranger and xgboost are multi-threaded themselves; parsnip pins them to 1 thread inside parallel tuning so they do not fight.
Seeds: set.seed() before the call gives reproducible results, sequential or parallel.

title: Resampling and tuning
text:
Nested cross-validation (when you need it)
Tuning on 5 folds and then reporting the best CV score is slightly optimistic — you picked the maximum of 20 noisy numbers.

Usually small (0.005–0.01 AUC) and the locked test set catches it. That is its job.
With small n, many candidates, or when there is no test set: nested CV — an outer loop of folds, and inside each outer analysis set a complete inner tuning. The outer assessment sets give an unbiased estimate of the whole procedure.
Cost: outer × inner × candidates model fits. tidymodels supports it via nested_cv() and a little purrr; TMwR has a worked chapter.


For a thesis: tune with repeated 10-fold, report the test set. For a methods paper or n < 500: nested CV.

title: Resampling and tuning
text:

TRIPOD+AI asks for, and reviewers increasingly check:

resampling scheme (k, repeats, stratification), seeds
which hyperparameters, what ranges, how searched, how selected (best vs 1-SE)
the CV estimate with SE and the test estimate — and that the test set was used once
performance by subgroup (sex, ethnicity, age band) — collect_predictions() |> group_by(...) |> roc_auc(...)

title: Support vector machines
section: Start with one variable: where do you put the line?
text:
Start with one variable: where do you put the line?



A threshold classifies. A point just over it is called “spicy” even though it looks like the “not spicy” group.


Maximal margin: put the threshold halfway between the closest members of each class — as far from both as possible.


Adapted from StatQuest (J. Starmer, 2019)

title: Support vector machines
section: Outliers break hard margins → soft margins
text:
Outliers break hard margins → soft margins



One outlier drags the maximal margin into a terrible place.


Soft margin: allow some points inside the margin, or on the wrong side, in exchange for a wider, more robust street. How many? Chosen by cross-validation → the cost parameter.

A soft-margin classifier is a support vector classifier. The support vectors are the few points that touch or cross the margin — the only ones that determine the boundary.

title: Support vector machines
section: Two dimensions, three dimensions, p dimensions
text:
Two dimensions, three dimensions, p dimensions






A line in 2-D, a plane in 3-D, a hyperplane in p-D. Same maths. Still straight.

title: Support vector machines
section: When a straight street cannot work: kernels
text:
When a straight street cannot work: kernels



No threshold on this axis separates the classes.

The kernel idea

Start in low dimension.
Map the data into a higher dimension (e.g. add \(x^2\)).
Find a straight hyperplane there.
Project back: the boundary is curved in the original space.

The kernel trick: you never compute the high-dimensional coordinates — only similarities between pairs of points — so even infinite dimensions are affordable.

title: Support vector machines
text:
Two kernels you will use


Polynomial — svm_poly(cost, degree) Boundary = polynomial curve. degree 1 = linear; 2–3 = gentle curves; higher = wiggly, overfits.
Radial basis function (RBF) — svm_rbf(cost, rbf_sigma) Similarity decays with distance like a Gaussian bump around each support vector → boundaries that can enclose islands. rbf_sigma: large = narrow bumps = wiggly; small = wide bumps = smooth.




Zhou (2017)

title: Support vector machines
text:
What the boundary looks like





A toy problem. On our age × bmi the pictures are far less dramatic — which is itself the finding: the risk surface is close to additive.

title: Support vector machines
text:
SVM in practice

svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |>
  set_engine("kernlab") |>
  set_mode("classification")








cost
penalty for margin violations. High → narrow margin, fits training data, overfits. Low → wide margin, underfits. Tune on a log₂ scale.


rbf_sigma / degree
boundary flexibility. Tune on a log₁₀ scale.


Pre-processing
numeric, scaled — mandatory. dm_rec does both. (kernlab also rescales internally by default — other engines don’t; keep it in the recipe.)


Probabilities
not native; kernlab fits a logistic on the decision values (“Platt scaling”) — slower, calibration so-so


Cost
roughly O(n²): fine at 4,000 rows, painful at 400,000


Interpretability
low: no coefficients (except linear), no trees, no importances without model-agnostic tools

title: Support vector machines
text:
Where SVMs fit today

State of the art for tabular data roughly 1995–2010; gradient boosting took that title, deep learning took images and text.
Still excellent for small, high-dimensional, clean problems: gene-expression panels, text classification, some signal problems.
The margin idea underpins a lot of later theory (regularisation as margin maximisation; kernel methods generally).
For survey-type health data you will rarely choose one over XGBoost — but you should be able to fit, tune and explain one when a reviewer asks.

title: The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow
section: R does not know what your numbers mean
text:
R does not know what your numbers mean

summary(nhms_raw$sys)        # Min. -9.0   <- nobody has a systolic BP of -9
table(nhms_raw$ethnic)       # 1 2 3 4 5   <- R will happily treat "Indian" as 1.5 x "Chinese"

Three things to fix before anything else:

Sentinel codes (-9, 999, -6) → NA: mutate(across(c(sys, dys, rbs, rchol), \(x) na_if(x, -9)))
Categorical codes → labelled factors: factor(ethnic, levels = 1:5, labels = c("Malay", ...))
The outcome → a factor with the event level first: factor(undx_dm, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No"))


Leave the -9s in and nothing crashes — that is the problem. The imputation step finds no NA to impute, the scaler learns a standard deviation inflated by impossible values, and every model downstream quietly absorbs the error. Silent data-cleaning misses are the most common defect in survey-based ML.

title: The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow
text:
The event-level rule

levels(nhms$undx_dm)
#> [1] "Yes" "No"


yardstick metrics assume the first level is the event of interest (event_level = "first").
Probability columns are named after the levels: .pred_Yes, .pred_No. Use .pred_Yes for ROC/PR/Brier.
If your data arrives as 0/1 with 1 = yes, the default factor order puts "0" first and your sensitivity and specificity silently swap.


Check levels(outcome)[1] every single time. Put it in your script template.

title: The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow
text:
Lock away a test set

set.seed(2026)
dm_split <- initial_split(dm_data, prop = 0.80, strata = undx_dm)
dm_train <- training(dm_split)   # 4,000 rows: everything happens here
dm_test  <- testing(dm_split)    # 1,000 rows: a final exam, sat ONCE, at the end of Day 2


prop: 75–80 % training is the convention; with 5,000 rows, 80/20 leaves ~115 cases in the test set — barely enough for a stable AUC. Smaller data → use resampling for everything and treat the test set as a formality.
strata: keeps the outcome prevalence equal in both halves. Always, for outcomes under ~30 %.
set.seed(): so you and your co-author get the same split.
Time-ordered data (forecasting)? Split by time, not at random: initial_time_split().
Clustered data (patients within clinics)? Split by cluster: group_initial_split().


Ask: “if you split patients at random but the same patient has 3 visits, what happens?” → leakage across split; group_initial_split.

title: The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow
section: The test set is a one-shot exam
text:
The test set is a one-shot exam
Every time you look at the test set and change something, it stops being a test set.

Model choice, hyperparameters, threshold, imputation strategy, which variables to keep → decided on resamples of the training set (Day 2).
The test set answers one question, once: “how well does the final pipeline do on data it never influenced?”
“We tried 12 models and report the best test AUC” is the single most common way papers overstate performance.

title: The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow
section: A recipe is a plan, not a result
text:
A recipe is a plan, not a result

dm_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>   # learn medians
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>     # learn modes
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>           # learn factor levels -> 0/1 columns
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>                      # learn which columns are constant
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())          # learn means and SDs









Verb
What it does
Who calls it




recipe() + step_*()
declares the plan; nothing computed
you


prep()
estimates the plan from the training data (medians, levels, means, SDs)
the workflow, on the analysis set of each fold


bake()
applies the estimated plan to any data (training, test, next year’s patients)
the workflow, at predict time




The test set is baked with training medians and SDs. The recipe is how tidymodels makes it structurally impossible to leak the test set into pre-processing.

text:

Need

section: Leakage: when the answer is in the inputs
text:
Leakage: when the answer is in the inputs

Target leakage = a predictor that would not be available — or would not have that value — at the moment the prediction is meant to be made, because it is caused by, measured with, or defined by the outcome.

In NHMS, undiagnosed diabetes is defined as “no known diagnosis and screening blood sugar ≥ threshold”. So rbs → undx_dm is not prediction. It is reading the label off the back of the card.








Leak
Looks like
Why it is a leak




rbs → undiagnosed DM
AUC 0.98
the measurement defines the outcome


“received metformin” → diabetes
AUC 0.99
treatment happens after diagnosis


“days in ICU” → in-hospital death
strong
known only at the end


patient ID / clinic code
mysteriously useful
encodes site, time, or case-mix


imputed with the full data, then split
+0.01–0.03 AUC
test rows shaped the imputation


same patient in train and test
+0.02–0.10
memorises the person, not the pattern

title: The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow
text:
The five-question leakage audit
Before you fit anything, for every predictor:

When is this value recorded relative to the outcome?
Would I have it at the moment I want to use the model (community, clinic, admission)?
Is it part of the definition of the outcome, or of its confirmation?
Does it change because of the outcome or its treatment?
Does it encode who/where/when rather than a biological or behavioural fact?

A “yes” to 3, 4 or 5, or a “no” to 2, means it comes out — however much AUC it costs.
While you are there: recodes of the same thing (pa is just pa_3cat == "Low") — keep one. Two copies add nothing and break linear models.

Our honest set for the diabetes question: everything a health volunteer could collect without a blood test or a BP cuff. Out: rbs, rchol, sys, dys, id, the other two outcomes.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A1 · You already own a neural network
text:
A1 · You already own a neural network
Logistic regression computes a weighted sum of the inputs, adds a constant, and squashes the result into (0, 1):
\[
p \;=\; \sigma(z), \qquad z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_p x_p + b, \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}.
\]
That object — weighted sum → bias → non-linear squash — is a neuron (or unit). \(w\) are its weights, \(b\) its bias, \(\sigma\) its activation function. Everything in deep learning is this unit, wired in different ways and trained by the same procedure.





Its limitation is geometric. The decision \(p \ge 0.5\) is the same as \(z \ge 0\), and \(z = 0\) is a straight line (a hyperplane in \(p\) dimensions). One neuron can only draw one straight boundary.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A2 · Why one neuron is not enough
text:
A2 · Why one neuron is not enough
Two classic problems defeat a straight line: XOR (positive when exactly one of two inputs is on) and the two rings below. No weights \(w_1, w_2, b\) exist that separate them. This is what Minsky and Papert pointed out in 1969, and it shut the field down for fifteen years — until people trained the obvious fix.





The fix: let several neurons each draw their own soft line, then let one more neuron combine those lines.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
text:
A3 · The multilayer perceptron (MLP)





Notation for one hidden layer of \(H\) units and one output unit, for a single person with inputs \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^p\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{z}^{(1)} &= \mathbf{W}^{(1)\top} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)} &&\text{(hidden pre-activations, } H \text{ numbers)}\\
\mathbf{a}^{(1)} &= g\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}\right) &&\text{(hidden activations; } g \text{ applied element-wise)}\\
z^{(2)} &= \mathbf{W}^{(2)\top} \mathbf{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)} &&\text{(output pre-activation, 1 number)}\\
p &= \sigma\!\left(z^{(2)}\right) &&\text{(predicted probability)}
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\) a \(p \times H\) matrix, \(\mathbf{b}^{(1)}\) a vector of \(H\) biases, \(\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\) a vector of \(H\) weights, \(b^{(2)}\) one bias. For \(n\) people at once, stack the inputs as rows of an \(n \times p\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) and everything becomes matrix multiplication — which is why GPUs matter and why the R code in Part B is five lines.
Parameter count: \(pH + H + H + 1\). For our data (\(p \approx 45\)) and \(H = 30\): \(45 \cdot 30 + 30 + 30 + 1 = 1{,}411\) free parameters, trained on ~3,200 people per fold. Hold that number — it explains Section A9.
“Deep” simply means more than one hidden layer: \(\mathbf{a}^{(2)} = g(\mathbf{W}^{(2)\top}\mathbf{a}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)})\), and so on. Each layer re-describes the previous one’s output; depth lets the network compose simple features into complex ones with far fewer units than one very wide layer would need.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
text:
A5 · The loss: what “wrong” means
For binary classification the loss is binary cross-entropy (log-loss), averaged over the \(n\) training people:
\[
L = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i \log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i) \,\Big].
\]
This is exactly the negative log-likelihood that logistic regression maximises — nothing new. It punishes confident wrong answers brutally (\(p = 0.99\) when \(y = 0\) costs 4.6; \(p = 0.6\) costs 0.9), and it is smooth, so it has a gradient everywhere. Accuracy has no gradient (a tiny weight change rarely flips a prediction), which is why nothing is trained on accuracy directly. Regression uses mean squared error; multi-class uses categorical cross-entropy; survival, ordinal and custom problems write their own.
For our worked example: \(L = -\log(0.5973) = 0.5154\).

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
text:
A6 · Gradient descent: walking downhill
Training = find the weights that minimise \(L\). There is no closed form, so we iterate:
\[
\theta \;\leftarrow\; \theta - \eta \,\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}
\qquad\text{for every weight and bias } \theta,
\]
where \(\eta\) is the learning rate. The gradient points uphill; we step the other way. Repeat for many epochs (passes through the data).













Variant
Gradient computed on
Comment




batch gradient descent
all \(n\) rows
exact; slow and memory-heavy for large \(n\) (what Part B and nnet do)


stochastic (SGD)
one row at a time
noisy; the noise helps escape poor regions


mini-batch
32–512 rows
the standard; one epoch = all mini-batches once (brulee, keras, torch)


momentum
running average of past gradients
rolls through flat regions; damps zig-zagging


Adam / AdamW
per-weight adaptive step + momentum
the default optimiser in most deep learning


L-BFGS
quasi-Newton (uses curvature)
excellent for small networks; nnet and brulee’s default



A learning-rate schedule (start higher, decay; or cyclic) often matters more than the choice of optimiser.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A7 · Backpropagation is the chain rule
text:
A7 · Backpropagation is the chain rule
We need \(\partial L / \partial \theta\) for every weight. Backpropagation computes them all in one backward sweep by applying the chain rule layer by layer, reusing each layer’s result for the layer before it. For one person (drop the \(1/n\)):
Output layer. With sigmoid output and cross-entropy loss, a small miracle: \[
\delta^{(2)} \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}} = p - y .
\] How wrong, with a sign. For our example: \(\delta^{(2)} = 0.5973 - 1 = -0.4027\).
Then, because \(z^{(2)} = \sum_h W^{(2)}_h a^{(1)}_h + b^{(2)}\): \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(2)}_h} = \delta^{(2)}\, a^{(1)}_h, \qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \delta^{(2)} .
\] Example: \(\partial L/\partial W^{(2)} = -0.4027 \times (0.6044,\ 0.1974) = (-0.2434,\ -0.0795)\); \(\partial L/\partial b^{(2)} = -0.4027\).
Pass the blame back. How much did each hidden activation contribute to the error? \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(1)}_h} = \delta^{(2)}\, W^{(2)}_h
\quad\Rightarrow\quad (-0.4027)(0.7,\ -0.4) = (-0.2819,\ 0.1611).
\]
Through the activation. \(a^{(1)}_h = \tanh(z^{(1)}_h)\), so multiply by \(\tanh'(z) = 1 - a^2\): \[
\delta^{(1)}_h \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(1)}_h} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(1)}_h}\,(1 - (a^{(1)}_h)^2)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad (-0.2819)(0.6347),\ (0.1611)(0.9610) = (-0.1789,\ 0.1548).
\]
Input weights. Because \(z^{(1)}_h = \sum_j W^{(1)}_{jh} x_j + b^{(1)}_h\): \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}_{jh}} = \delta^{(1)}_h\, x_j, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(1)}_h} = \delta^{(1)}_h .
\] Example: \(\partial L / \partial \mathbf{W}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.0 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}(-0.1789,\ 0.1548) =
\begin{pmatrix} -0.1789 & 0.1548 \\ -0.0895 & 0.0774 \end{pmatrix}\).
One gradient-descent step with \(\eta = 0.5\) (\(\theta \leftarrow \theta - 0.5\,\partial L/\partial\theta\)):
\[
\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \to \begin{pmatrix} 0.5895 & -0.3774 \\ 0.2447 & 0.7613 \end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathbf{b}^{(1)} \to (0.1895,\ 0.0226),\quad
\mathbf{W}^{(2)} \to (0.8217,\ -0.3603),\quad b^{(2)} \to 0.2514 .
\]
Run the forward pass again with the new weights: \(p = 0.6966\), loss \(0.3615\) (was 0.5154). The network moved toward the right answer for this person. Do that for all \(n\) people (average the gradients), thousands of times, and it has learned. That is all “learning” means here: the numbers in \(\mathbf{W}\) changed.






In matrix form, for \(n\) people (this is Part B’s code)



\(\;\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)} = (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{y})/n\) · \(\;\nabla_{\mathbf{W}^{(2)}} = \mathbf{A}^{(1)\top}\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)}\) · \(\;\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)} = \big(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)}\mathbf{W}^{(2)\top}\big) \odot (1 - \mathbf{A}^{(1)2})\) · \(\;\nabla_{\mathbf{W}^{(1)}} = \mathbf{X}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)}\) · biases are column sums of the \(\boldsymbol{\delta}\)s.


Deep-learning frameworks (torch, TensorFlow, JAX) do this automatically for any architecture — automatic differentiation. You write the forward pass; they derive the backward pass. The maths does not change.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A8 · Making training work: initialisation and gradient flow
text:
A8 · Making training work: initialisation and gradient flow

Initialisation. Weights start small and random (never all zero — identical units would receive identical gradients and never differentiate). Modern schemes (Xavier/Glorot for tanh, He for ReLU) scale the randomness to the number of inputs so activations neither explode nor vanish layer by layer. Different seeds → slightly different networks; report that.
Vanishing / exploding gradients. Each backward step multiplies by a weight and an activation derivative. Products of many small numbers → 0 (deep sigmoid nets stall); of many large ones → ∞ (training diverges). Fixes: ReLU, good initialisation, gradient clipping, batch normalisation (standardise each layer’s inputs during training), residual connections (let a layer learn a correction to its input rather than a full transform).
Scaling the inputs is not optional. Gradient descent on hh_income in ringgit and age in years will spend all its steps on income. step_normalize().

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A9 · Capacity, overfitting and the brakes
text:
A9 · Capacity, overfitting and the brakes
A network with 1,411 parameters on 3,200 people will, left alone, drive the training loss toward zero by memorising — validation AUC falls, probabilities pile up at 0 and 1. The regularisers:








Brake
Mechanism
parsnip / brulee




weight decay (L2)
add \(\lambda\sum\theta^2\) to the loss, so the gradient step also shrinks every weight toward 0: the network’s ridge regression
penalty


dropout
during training, silence a random fraction of hidden units on every step; at test time use all of them, scaled. Forces redundancy; approximates an ensemble
dropout (brulee)


early stopping
watch a validation slice; stop when its loss has not improved for k epochs
brulee: stop_iter, validation


smaller architecture
fewer units / layers
hidden_units


batch normalisation
stabilises and mildly regularises
brulee option


data augmentation
more (perturbed) training examples
images, audio



Rules of thumb: always use early stopping when you can; use weight decay or dropout (brulee asks you not to combine them); tune width and decay together — they trade off.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A10 · Architecture choices for tabular data
text:
A10 · Architecture choices for tabular data

Width: 8–64 hidden units for a few thousand rows; the data, not the problem, set the ceiling.
Depth: one hidden layer is usually enough for tabular data; two (e.g. 32 → 16) occasionally helps; more rarely does.
Activation: ReLU for depth; tanh/sigmoid fine for one small layer (nnet).
Output: sigmoid + cross-entropy for binary; softmax for multi-class; identity + MSE for regression. parsnip sets this from set_mode().
Hyperparameters that matter, in order: learning rate (if not L-BFGS) → width → weight decay/dropout → epochs (with early stopping) → batch size → depth.

Universal approximation (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991): one hidden layer with enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain. “Enough” can be astronomically many; depth achieves the same with far fewer parameters. The theorem says a network can represent the truth, not that gradient descent will find it or that your 3,200 people will identify it.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A11 · Beyond the MLP (what “deep learning” adds)
text:
A11 · Beyond the MLP (what “deep learning” adds)








Architecture
Core idea
Health examples




Convolutional network (CNN)
a small filter (3 × 3 weights) slides over the image, firing where it matches a pattern; layers of filters build edges → textures → parts → objects; pooling shrinks and adds translation invariance
fundus photos (diabetic retinopathy), chest X-ray triage, pathology slides, dermatology, 1-D CNNs on ECG


Recurrent network (RNN, LSTM, GRU)
processes a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state (memory); LSTM gates control what to keep
ECG/EEG, vital-sign streams, early sequence models of EHR visits


Transformer / attention
every position looks at every other position and learns where to look; no recurrence, massively parallel; the basis of BERT/GPT and modern vision models
clinical notes, coding, EHR trajectories, foundation models for imaging and text


Autoencoder
compress to a bottleneck and reconstruct; learns a low-dimensional representation
denoising, anomaly detection, phenotype discovery


Transfer learning
start from a network trained on millions of natural images or documents; retrain only the last layers on your 2,000 examples
how small medical imaging datasets get state-of-the-art results



The common thread: the inputs are raw and high-dimensional (pixels, waveforms, tokens) and the useful features must be learned. Tabular survey data already arrives feature-engineered — which is why trees do so well on it.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A12 · When neural networks lose: the evidence on tabular data
text:
A12 · When neural networks lose: the evidence on tabular data







Study
Finding




Shwartz-Ziv & Armon 2022, Information Fusion — “Tabular data: deep learning is not all you need”
XGBoost beat the deep tabular models on the datasets those models were published with


Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux 2022, NeurIPS — “Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?”
45 datasets: tuned GBMs win on medium-sized tabular data; nets struggle with uninformative features and non-smooth targets


McElfresh et al. 2023, NeurIPS — “When do neural nets outperform boosted trees on tabular data?”
176 datasets: for most, the gap is smaller than the gain from tuning; nets win on some large, smooth problems


Christodoulou et al. 2019, J Clin Epidemiol
no performance benefit of ML over logistic regression across 71 clinical prediction studies, after accounting for bias



On 5,000 rows of survey data a well-regularised network ties boosted trees and logistic regression — and costs more compute, more tuning, more run-to-run variance and less interpretability. Part C shows exactly that. It is a finding, not a failure. Where networks earn their keep is A11.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: A13 · How deep learning fails in health (same medicine as Day 1)
text:
A13 · How deep learning fails in health (same medicine as Day 1)
Shortcut learning (the pneumonia classifier that read the portable-X-ray marker; COVID chest X-ray models that learned the hospital — DeGrave et al. 2021), dataset shift (a new scanner, a new population), over-confidence (deep nets are badly calibrated out of the box — Guo et al. 2017; recalibrate), data and label hunger, reproducibility (seeds, GPU non-determinism), equity (under-performance on under-represented skin tones, sexes, ethnicities unless measured). Leak-free splits by patient, honest resampling, calibration, subgroup checks, and explanations used as audits — the whole workshop applies unchanged.

section: B2 · The network: 2 inputs → 8 tanh units → 1 sigmoid output
text:
B2 · The network: 2 inputs → 8 tanh units → 1 sigmoid output

sigmoid <- function(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
H  <- 8          # hidden units
lr <- 0.5        # learning rate

set.seed(1)
W1 <- matrix(rnorm(2 * H, sd = 0.5), nrow = 2, ncol = H); b1 <- rep(0, H)   # input  -> hidden
W2 <- matrix(rnorm(H, sd = 0.5), nrow = H, ncol = 1);     b2 <- 0           # hidden -> output

forward <- function(X, W1, b1, W2, b2) {
  Z1 <- sweep(X %*% W1, 2, b1, "+")   # weighted sums, hidden layer         (n x H)
  A1 <- tanh(Z1)                       # activation - this is what bends the boundary
  Z2 <- A1 %*% W2 + b2                 # weighted sum, output                (n x 1)
  P  <- sigmoid(Z2)                    # probability of "inner"
  list(A1 = A1, P = P)
}

loss_hist <- numeric(0); snapshots <- list()
for (epoch in 1:500) {
  fw <- forward(X, W1, b1, W2, b2); P <- fw$P; A1 <- fw$A1
  loss_hist[epoch] <- -mean(y * log(P + 1e-9) + (1 - y) * log(1 - P + 1e-9))   # cross-entropy (A5)

  # BACKPROPAGATION (A7), in matrix form
  dZ2 <- (P - y) / n                   # delta at the output
  dW2 <- t(A1) %*% dZ2;  db2 <- sum(dZ2)
  dA1 <- dZ2 %*% t(W2)                 # pass the blame back through W2
  dZ1 <- dA1 * (1 - A1^2)              # through tanh (derivative 1 - a^2)
  dW1 <- t(X) %*% dZ1;   db1 <- colSums(dZ1)

  # GRADIENT DESCENT (A6)
  W1 <- W1 - lr * dW1; b1 <- b1 - lr * db1
  W2 <- W2 - lr * dW2; b2 <- b2 - lr * db2

  if (epoch %in% c(1, 10, 50, 500)) snapshots[[as.character(epoch)]] <- list(W1 = W1, b1 = b1, W2 = W2, b2 = b2)
}

tibble(epoch = seq_along(loss_hist), loss = loss_hist) |>
  ggplot(aes(epoch, loss)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Training loss: gradient descent walking downhill")

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
section: C5 · Explain the network with this morning’s plots
text:
C5 · Explain the network with this morning’s plots
There is no TreeSHAP for a network, so this is where KernelSHAP earns its keep: it estimates the Shapley values from predictions alone, for any model. Two things keep it affordable. First, explain a sample of people against a small background sample — cost grows with rows × background × the number of rounds it needs to converge, and a network needs more rounds than a tree ensemble. Second, hand it the baked matrix and the bare model, not the whole workflow: every one of the thousands of prediction calls would otherwise re-run the recipe. As this morning, collapse adds each factor’s dummy columns back together and X supplies the original values for the plots.

set.seed(2026)
X_explain <- dm_train |> select(-undx_dm) |> slice_sample(n = 60)           # people to explain (KernelSHAP is the one slow chunk - keep it small)
X_bg      <- dm_train |> select(-undx_dm) |> slice_sample(n = 30)           # background ("what a typical person looks like")

rec_fit  <- extract_recipe(nn_fit)                                          # trained recipe
nn_model <- extract_fit_parsnip(nn_fit)                                     # bare model: predicts on BAKED data
X_baked  <- bake(rec_fit, new_data = X_explain, all_predictors())
bg_baked <- bake(rec_fit, new_data = X_bg,      all_predictors())
pred_yes_baked <- function(model, newdata, ...) predict(model, new_data = newdata, type = "prob")$.pred_Yes

dummy_step <- tidy(rec_fit) |> filter(type == "dummy") |> pull(number)
facs       <- tidy(rec_fit, number = dummy_step) |> pull(terms) |> unique()   # the original factor columns
# each factor -> the dummy columns it produced. bake() cleans the level names (25-29.9 -> X25.29.9), so match on
# the "<factor>_" prefix of the ACTUAL baked columns rather than on the raw level names.
collapse   <- setNames(lapply(facs, \(f) grep(paste0("^", f, "_"), colnames(X_baked), value = TRUE)), facs)
collapse   <- collapse[lengths(collapse) > 0]

t_shap <- system.time(
  ks_nn <- kernelshap(nn_model, X = X_baked, bg_X = bg_baked, pred_fun = pred_yes_baked, verbose = FALSE)
)
t_shap[["elapsed"]]                                                         # seconds

[1] 207.57

sv_nn <- shapviz(ks_nn, X = X_explain, collapse = collapse)
sv_importance(sv_nn, kind = "beeswarm", max_display = 15) + labs(title = "SHAP: tuned neural network")







sv_dependence(sv_nn, v = "bmi", color_var = "fam_hx_dm") + labs(title = "Network: BMI x family history")








Does the network find the same structure the trees found this morning? Agreement across two very different model families is evidence the structure is in the data, not an artefact of one algorithm.

text:
Your turn (25 min)






Task A · Count the parameters, then watch them overfit




How many weights does nn(40, 0) have? (inputs × hidden + hidden + hidden + 1; inputs = columns out of dm_rec.) How many people are in a training fold?
Resample nn(4, 0.01), nn(40, 0) and nn(40, 0.05) in one workflow_set(). Which has the worst Brier score, and why does weight decay fix it?









Solution A






n_in <- dm_rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> select(-undx_dm) |> ncol()
c(inputs = n_in, weights = n_in * 40 + 40 + 40 + 1, people_per_fold = round(nrow(dm_train) * 4 / 5))

         inputs         weights people_per_fold 
             45            1881            3199 

set.seed(2026)
nn_three <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec),
                         models = list(small = nn(4, 0.01), big_free = nn(40, 0), big_decay = nn(40, 0.05))) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)
collect_metrics(nn_three) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)


  



About 1,900 weights for ~3,200 people — under two people per parameter. big_free has the worst Brier: it produces over-confident probabilities near 0 and 1 for the wrong people. Weight decay shrinks the weights so the network cannot build extreme logits out of noise — the same idea as ridge regression.









Task B · Does it see the same world?



Compare the top-8 SHAP features of sv_nn with the XGBoost beeswarm from Tutorial 6. Where they agree, what does that buy you? Where they disagree, which do you believe, and how would you find out?








Solution B





Agreement on age, BMI/waist, family history and ethnicity across two unrelated model families is evidence the structure is real. Disagreement on minor features is usually noise: refit both on bootstrap resamples and see whether the ranking is stable before telling a story about it.









Task C · Stretch (needs torch)




Change activation in deep_spec to "tanh" and to "elu". Does anything change on this data? Why so little?
Set dropout = 0 and penalty = 0.01 instead. Compare the loss curves (autoplot()): which stops earlier?
Try hidden_units = c(64L, 32L, 16L). Better, worse, or the same — and what does that tell you about the data, not the network?









Solution C (discussion)






Barely anything: with one or two small layers and scaled inputs, the activation shape is not the binding constraint — the amount of signal in 4,000 rows is. 2. Weight decay typically trains more smoothly and stops a little later; dropout’s noisier loss curve is normal. 3. The same within noise, slower, more variable: the extra capacity has nothing to learn. On tabular data of this size, capacity is not the bottleneck; information is.

section: Take-home challenge: who has undiagnosed hypertension?
text:
Take-home challenge: who has undiagnosed hypertension?
Half of Malaysian adults with hypertension do not know it. Build a community screening tool for undx_hpt with budget to measure the blood pressure of one adult in three. Everything you need is in Tutorials 1–7:

Leakage audit (sys and dys define the outcome; what else goes?).
Stratified split, five folds, recipe.
Bake-off: logistic, random forest, SVM, XGBoost, mlp() — same folds.
Race-tune the winner; one-SE rule.
Threshold that flags one in three, chosen on CV predictions; sensitivity, PPV and number-needed-to-measure on the test set, once.
Calibration plot; SHAP beeswarm; one dependence plot (try age coloured by sex).
Two caveats (prevalence shift; synthetic data).

Expected honest AUC ≈ 0.81–0.83. If you see 0.95, go back to step 1. The simulator’s truth is in data-raw/simulate_nhms_synthetic.py — read it after you have finished, and check whether your SHAP plots found the interactions it planted.

title: Tutorial 7 · Neural networks
text:
What to remember

A neuron = weighted sum + non-linear squash. Logistic regression is one neuron. A hidden layer bends the line.
Training = gradient descent on a loss; backpropagation is the chain rule, layer by layer, reusing each result.
Networks overfit by default; weight decay, dropout and early stopping are the brakes; scaled inputs are mandatory.
mlp() + nnet: tune width and decay like any other parsnip model; brulee for depth.
On small tabular data networks tie boosted trees and lose on cost. They win on images, signals, text, sequences.

title: Tutorial 5 · Resampling and tuning
text:
What you will do



See with your own eyes that a single train/test split is a noisy measurement; meet the resampling menu; mark XGBoost’s hyperparameters with tune(), define a search space, search it with a grid and then with racing; pick a winner with the one-standard-error rule; and finally touch the test set once with last_fit().
Time: 25 min live coding + 10 min Your turn.

title: Tutorial 5 · Resampling and tuning
text:
1 · Why one split lies
The same logistic model, 25 different random 80/20 splits:

set.seed(1)
many_splits <- mc_cv(dm_data, prop = 0.80, times = 25, strata = undx_dm)   # Monte-Carlo CV = repeated random splits

set.seed(1)
lr_many <- fit_resamples(lr_wf, many_splits, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))

collect_metrics(lr_many, summarize = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(.estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "#0b4f6c") +
  labs(x = "test-set AUC", y = NULL, title = "Same model, 25 random splits",
       subtitle = "Whoever reported the maximum would be lying by accident") +
  theme_minimal()







collect_metrics(lr_many)     # mean and std_err: THIS is what to report


  



Nothing changed but which 1,000 people were held out. Any number in that spread is a legitimate “test-set AUC”. A paper that reports the top of it is not lying; it is reporting one draw from a distribution and calling it the answer. With ~115 cases in a test set the spread is unavoidable.






Important



Report mean ± standard error across resamples. The SE is the number that tells you whether two models differ.

Scheme

Use when

you can afford it; lowers the variance of the estimate

always, for outcomes under ~30 %

Look inside one fold:

dm_folds$splits[[1]]

<Analysis/Assess/Total>
<3198/801/3999>

analysis(dm_folds$splits[[1]])   |> nrow()    # the 4/5 used for fitting: recipe prepped HERE, model fitted HERE

[1] 3198

assessment(dm_folds$splits[[1]]) |> nrow()    # the 1/5 held out: baked with the analysis set's medians and SDs

[1] 801


Imputation medians, scaling, dummy levels, SMOTE, feature selection — everything estimated from data is re-estimated on the analysis set, five separate times. That is why pre-processing lives in a recipe inside a workflow and not in a mutate() before the split.

title: Tutorial 5 · Resampling and tuning
text:
3 · Tuning: mark, bound, search

Mark what to tune

xgb_tune_spec <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune(), sample_size = tune()) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |>
  set_mode("classification")

xgb_tune_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, xgb_tune_spec)

tune() is a placeholder. The workflow is complete but cannot be fit() until the placeholders are filled.


Bound the search space (dials)

xgb_params <- extract_parameter_set_dials(xgb_tune_wf) |>
  update(
    learn_rate  = learn_rate(range = c(-2.5, -0.5)),    # log10 scale -> 0.003 .. 0.32
    tree_depth  = tree_depth(range = c(2L, 8L)),
    min_n       = min_n(range = c(5L, 60L)),
    sample_size = sample_prop(range = c(0.5, 1))
  )
xgb_params


  



Every tunable argument has a dials object with a default range and, where sensible, a log transform (learn_rate, penalty, cost, rbf_sigma). Tune those on the log scale or you waste most of the grid at one end. Defaults are deliberately wide — narrow them with domain sense. Ranges that depend on the data (mtry ≤ number of predictors) need finalize() or an explicit update().


Lay out the candidates

grid_regular(xgb_params, levels = 3) |> nrow()          # 3^4 = 81 candidates, only 3 distinct values each

[1] 81

set.seed(2026)
xgb_grid <- grid_space_filling(xgb_params, size = 20)   # 20 candidates spread evenly over the 4-D space
xgb_grid


  










Search: every candidate × every fold

set.seed(2026)
t0 <- Sys.time()
xgb_tuned <- tune_grid(xgb_tune_wf, resamples = dm_folds, grid = xgb_grid,
                       metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class), control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE))
Sys.time() - t0

Time difference of 1.040263 mins

collect_metrics(xgb_tuned) |> filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |> arrange(desc(mean)) |> head()


  


autoplot(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc") + theme_minimal()








Read the panels: a flat panel means that parameter does not matter much in this range; a slope or peak tells you where to look next. Learning rate is almost always the one that matters.


Choose

show_best(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)


  


select_best(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc")                                      # numerically best


  


select_by_one_std_err(xgb_tuned, metric = "roc_auc", tree_depth, desc(min_n))   # SIMPLEST within 1 SE of best


  









The one-standard-error rule



Among candidates whose score is within one standard error of the best, choose the simplest (shallower trees, larger leaves, more regularisation). Simpler = less overfit, faster, easier to explain — and the “best” was probably best by luck. The sorting arguments define what “simpler” means.

4 · Racing: stop wasting folds on hopeless candidates

set.seed(2026)
t0 <- Sys.time()
xgb_race <- tune_race_anova(xgb_tune_wf, resamples = dm_folds, param_info = xgb_params, grid = 30,
                            metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class),

Sys.time() - t0

Time difference of 53.47074 secs

plot_race(xgb_race) + theme_minimal()







show_best(xgb_race, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)


  



After the first three folds an ANOVA model asks, for each candidate, “is this one significantly worse than the leader?” — and if so, drops it. Thirty candidates in about the time twenty took, same answer.

section: 6 · Two things to know, not to do today
text:
6 · Two things to know, not to do today
Nested cross-validation. Picking the best of 30 noisy candidates and reporting its CV score is slightly optimistic. Usually small (≤ 0.01 AUC) and the locked test set catches it. With small n, many candidates, or no test set, run an outer loop of folds and do the whole tuning inside each — nested_cv() plus a little purrr; TMwR has a worked chapter.
Parallel processing changed. tune ≥ 1.3 uses the future framework. doParallel::registerDoParallel() from older notes does nothing now. plan(multisession, workers = n) is all you need; stop at 3–4 workers on an 8 GB laptop.

top

title: Tutorial 3 · Support vector machines
text:
1 · The idea, in four pictures






In one paragraph



Start with one predictor and two classes. A threshold classifies, but a point just over it is called positive even when it looks like the negatives. The maximal-margin classifier puts the boundary halfway between the closest members of the two classes — as far from both as possible. One outlier drags that boundary into a terrible place, so we allow some points inside the margin or on the wrong side: a soft margin, whose generosity is set by cross-validation. That is a support vector classifier; the support vectors are the few points that touch or cross the margin — the only ones that matter. In two dimensions the boundary is a line, in three a plane, in p a hyperplane — still straight. When the classes overlap so that no straight boundary works, a kernel maps the data into a higher dimension where they are separable by a hyperplane, and the boundary projected back is curved. The kernel trick means you never compute the high-dimensional coordinates, only similarities between pairs of points.







Two kernels you will use:









Kernel
parsnip
Shape
Flexibility knob




Linear
svm_linear(cost)
hyperplane
—


Polynomial
svm_poly(cost, degree, scale_factor)
polynomial curve
degree: 1 = linear, 2–3 = gentle curves, higher = wiggly


Radial basis (RBF)
svm_rbf(cost, rbf_sigma)
Gaussian bumps around support vectors; can enclose islands
rbf_sigma: large = narrow bumps = wiggly; small = wide bumps = smooth



And the knob every kernel shares: cost — the penalty for a point violating the margin. High cost → narrow margin, fits the training data closely, overfits. Low cost → wide margin, underfits. Tune it on a log₂ scale.

section: 2 · What an SVM needs from the recipe
text:
2 · What an SVM needs from the recipe
Two non-negotiables:

Numeric predictors — SVMs compute distances; “Indian” has no distance from “Malay”. step_dummy().
Scaled predictors — otherwise hh_income (thousands) defines the distance and age (tens) is ignored. step_normalize().

dm_rec already does both, which is why it was written that way in Tutorial 1. One engine-specific wrinkle: kernlab::ksvm() quietly standardises numeric inputs itself (scaled = TRUE is its default), so with this engine an unscaled recipe is rescued behind your back. Other SVM implementations (LiblineaR, e1071 with scale = FALSE, anything you write in Python) do not, and neither do the neural networks this afternoon — keep the scaling in the recipe, where it is visible, versioned and applied identically at prediction time.

dm_rec

text:
3 · Three kernels, one workflow

svm_lin_spec  <- svm_linear(cost = 1) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification")
svm_poly_spec <- svm_poly(cost = 1, degree = 2) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification")
svm_rbf_spec  <- svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification")

rbf_sigma = 0.005 is a reasonable start for ~45 scaled predictors (kernlab’s own heuristic, sigest(), lands nearby). Leave it out and kernlab estimates it for you.
Fit the RBF version once and look at what came back:

SVMs do not produce probabilities natively; this Platt scaling is a bolt-on, and its calibration is so-so (Tutorial 6 will show you how to check).

augment(svm_rbf_fit, dm_train) |> cls_metrics(truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_Yes)

Three things to notice while it runs:

It is slower than the forest. SVM training cost grows roughly with n² (every pair of points enters the kernel matrix). 4,000 rows is fine; 400,000 is not. The probability model roughly doubles the time again.
The kernels are usually within one standard error of each other here — and of this morning’s logistic regression. The simulated truth is close to additive with a few interactions, and a linear SVM on 45 scaled dummies is, in effect, a regularised logistic regression.
Nothing in the output tells you why a person was classified. No coefficients you can read (except for the linear kernel), no trees, no importances without the model-agnostic tools of Tutorial 6.

title: Tutorial 3 · Support vector machines
text:
5 · Where SVMs fit today
SVMs were the best general-purpose classifier from roughly 1995 to 2010. Gradient boosting took that title for tabular data (tomorrow morning) and deep learning took it for images and text. They remain excellent for small, high-dimensional, clean problems — gene-expression panels, text classification, some signal problems — and the margin idea underpins a lot of later theory. For survey-type health data you will rarely choose one over XGBoost, but you should be able to fit, tune and explain one when a reviewer asks.

title: Tutorial 3 · Support vector machines
text:
Your turn (15 min)






Task A · Cost and overfitting



Fit svm_rbf(cost = ___, rbf_sigma = 0.005) for cost in {0.1, 1, 10, 100} with fit_resamples() on dm_folds (use a workflow_set() so it is one call). For each, also record the training-set AUC from a plain fit() on dm_train. Plot or tabulate training AUC and CV AUC against cost.
A1. Which direction does the gap between training and CV AUC move as cost rises? Why? A2. Which cost would you pick, and would you want to try values outside this range?








Solution A






costs <- c(0.1, 1, 10, 100)
svm_costs <- lapply(costs, \(cst) svm_rbf(cost = cst, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification"))
names(svm_costs) <- paste0("cost_", costs)

set.seed(2026)
cost_cv <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = svm_costs) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc), seed = 2026)

cv_auc <- collect_metrics(cost_cv) |>
  transmute(cost = readr::parse_number(wflow_id), cv_auc = mean, se = std_err)

train_auc <- tibble(
  cost = costs,
  train_auc = sapply(svm_costs, \(spec) workflow(dm_rec, spec) |> fit(dm_train) |>
                       augment(dm_train) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> pull(.estimate))
)

left_join(cv_auc, train_auc, by = "cost")


  



A1: training AUC climbs toward 1 as cost rises (the margin narrows and the boundary bends around individual points) while CV AUC flattens or falls — the classic overfitting gap. A2: the CV optimum is usually at cost ≈ 1 or below; it is worth probing 0.01–0.3 as well. This is exactly what tune_grid() automates tomorrow, on a log scale.









Task B · What happens without scaling? (5 min)



Build rec_noscale = dm_rec without step_normalize() (impute, dummy, zv only). Because kernlab would silently rescale for you, switch that off with set_engine("kernlab", scaled = FALSE) so you see what the kernel actually does with raw units. Resample and compare the CV AUC with the scaled version.








Solution B






rec_noscale <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

svm_raw_spec <- svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |>
  set_engine("kernlab", scaled = FALSE) |>      # stop kernlab from standardising internally
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(2026)
noscale_res <- fit_resamples(workflow(rec_noscale, svm_raw_spec), dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class))
collect_metrics(noscale_res)


  



Noticeably worse: with hh_income in ringgit dominating every distance, the kernel “sees” income and little else. Scaling is not a nicety for distance-based methods (SVMs, neural networks); it is part of the model. (Had you left kernlab’s default scaled = TRUE, the two recipes would have tied — and you would have learned the wrong lesson. Know what your engine does for you.)

title: Tutorial 3 · Support vector machines
text:
What to remember

SVM = widest possible street between the classes, with a cost-controlled tolerance for violations.
Kernels bend the street; rbf_sigma/degree set how much. Both knobs need tuning on a log scale.
Numeric + scaled inputs are mandatory. Probabilities are a bolt-on; check their calibration.
Slow for large n; opaque without model-agnostic explanation tools.

The event-level rule

text:
4 · The naive model — a deliberate mistake
Throw everything in and see what happens.

naive_data <- nhms |> select(-id, -undx_hpt, -undx_chol, -pa)   # `pa` is an exact recode of pa_3cat; keep one copy

set.seed(2026)
naive_split <- initial_split(naive_data, prop = 0.80, strata = undx_dm)
naive_train <- training(naive_split)
naive_test  <- testing(naive_split)

naive_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = naive_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

lr_spec <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> set_mode("classification")

naive_fit <- workflow(naive_rec, lr_spec) |> fit(data = naive_train)

naive_preds <- augment(naive_fit, new_data = naive_test)   # test data + .pred_class + .pred_Yes + .pred_No
roc_auc(naive_preds, truth = undx_dm, .pred_Yes)


  



An AUC near 0.98. If a screening model for undiagnosed diabetes ever gives you that, you have not built a brilliant model — you have leaked the answer. Which variable is doing it?

tidy(naive_fit) |> arrange(desc(abs(statistic))) |> head(8)


  



rbs — random blood sugar. In NHMS, undiagnosed diabetes is defined as “no known diagnosis and screening blood sugar above threshold”. rbs sits on both sides of the equation. By the time you have an rbs you do not need a model.






Target leakage



A predictor leaks when it would not be available — or would not have that value — at the moment the prediction is meant to be made, because it is caused by, measured with, or defined by the outcome.








Leak
Looks like
Why




rbs → undiagnosed DM
AUC 0.98
the measurement defines the outcome


“on metformin” → diabetes
AUC 0.99
treatment follows diagnosis


“days in ICU” → in-hospital death
strong
known only at the end


patient ID / clinic code
mysteriously useful
encodes site, time or case-mix


imputing on the full data, then splitting
+0.01–0.03 AUC
test rows shaped the imputation


same patient in train and test
+0.02–0.10
memorises the person, not the pattern



Five questions for every predictor: (1) When is it recorded relative to the outcome? (2) Would I have it when I want to use the model? (3) Is it part of the outcome’s definition or confirmation? (4) Does it change because of the outcome or its treatment? (5) Does it encode who/where/when rather than a fact about the person?

Our use case is a community screening tool: things a health volunteer could collect without a blood test or a BP cuff. strata = undx_dm keeps the prevalence identical in both halves. Always do this for outcomes under ~30 %: without it a lucky split gives 9 % in one half and 14 % in the other and your metrics move for no real reason.
set.seed() so that you and your co-author get the same split.
The test set is a one-shot exam. Every decision from here on — model, hyperparameters, threshold, imputation strategy — is made on resamples of dm_train. dm_test is touched once, at the end of Tutorial 5.
Time-ordered data? Split by time (initial_time_split()). Repeated measures? Split by person (group_initial_split()).

section: 7 · The recipe: a plan, estimated later
text:
7 · The recipe: a plan, estimated later

dm_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>   # numeric NAs -> median of the TRAINING data
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>     # factor NAs  -> most common level
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>           # factors -> 0/1 indicator columns
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>                      # drop constant columns (dm, hpt, chol are all 0)
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())          # centre + scale: needed by SVM and NN; harmless for trees

dm_rec

Nothing has been computed yet. A recipe is a plan; prep() estimates the plan from the training data (the medians, the levels, the means and SDs) and bake() applies it to any data. You will rarely call these yourself — the workflow does — but once, look inside:

dm_prep     <- prep(dm_rec)
baked_train <- bake(dm_prep, new_data = NULL)      # NULL = the data it was prepped on
baked_test  <- bake(dm_prep, new_data = dm_test)   # the TEST set, transformed with TRAINING medians and SDs

dim(dm_train); dim(baked_train)                    # 33 columns in, ~46 out (dummies), 3 zero-variance gone

[1] 3999   33


[1] 3999   46

tidy(dm_prep, number = 1) |> head()                # the medians that were learned


  


tidy(dm_prep, number = 5) |> filter(terms == "age")# the mean and SD that were learned


  









Step order matters




step_indicate_na() — before anything removes the NAs
step_impute_*() — before dummies (mode on factors) and before scaling (medians in raw units)
step_other(), step_novel() — before step_dummy()
step_dummy()
step_interact(), step_ns() — on the dummy columns
step_zv() / step_nzv() / step_lincomb() — after dummies
step_normalize() — last, so everything the model sees is on one scale
themis::step_smote() etc. — last of all, training data only (skip = TRUE is the default)

Your turn (45 min, in pairs)






Task A · The leakage audit (10 min, no code)



For each variable, write keep / drop and one reason, from the point of view of a volunteer at a pasar malam with a tape measure and a questionnaire:



Variable
Keep?
Reason




rbs




sys, dys




rchol




bmi, waist




fam_hx_dm




id




undx_hpt, undx_chol




dm, hpt, chol




pa and pa_3cat

(hint: count(nhms, pa, pa_3cat))











Solution A





rbs — drop: it defines the outcome. sys, dys, rchol — drop: not available before the test, and they define the other two outcomes. bmi, waist — keep: a tape measure and scales. fam_hx_dm — keep: one question. id — drop: an identifier. undx_hpt, undx_chol — drop: other outcomes measured at the same visit. dm, hpt, chol — all zero by construction (nobody with a known diagnosis is in this sample); step_zv() removes them. pa vs pa_3cat — count() shows pa == "Inactive" exactly when pa_3cat == "Low": one is a recode of the other. Keep the three-level version; two copies add nothing and make linear models rank-deficient (recipes::step_lincomb() would catch this automatically).









Task B · Two recipes, one model (25 min)



Recipe A is dm_rec. Recipe B remembers which values were missing and uses k-nearest-neighbour imputation. Resample both with the same logistic model on the same five folds and compare.

rec_b <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_indicate_na(bmi, waist, occupation) |>          # B1. why must this come BEFORE imputation?
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>                           # constant columns would confuse the distance below
  step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = ___) |>  # B2. try 5
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

rec_b |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> glimpse()   # B3. which new columns appeared?

set.seed(2026)
res_a <- fit_resamples(workflow(dm_rec, lr_spec), resamples = ___, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class))
set.seed(2026)

bind_rows(median_mode = collect_metrics(res_a), knn_indicator = collect_metrics(res_b), .id = "recipe") |>
  select(recipe, .metric, mean, std_err)

B4. Is the difference bigger than the standard error? What does that say about how much imputation strategy matters here (7 % missing, MAR)? When would it matter a lot?








Solution B






rec_b <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_indicate_na(bmi, waist, occupation) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

rec_b |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> select(starts_with("na_ind")) |> head(3)


  


set.seed(2026)
res_a <- fit_resamples(workflow(dm_rec, lr_spec), resamples = dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class))
set.seed(2026)

B1: after imputation there is nothing left to indicate. B3: na_ind_bmi, na_ind_waist, na_ind_occupation. B4: the two recipes are within one standard error of each other. With 7 % MAR missingness in predictors of modest importance, the imputation method barely matters. It matters when missingness is heavy, informative (MNAR — e.g. people who skip the weight question because of their weight), or sits in your strongest predictor; the missing-indicator is how you let a model use informative missingness.

tidy(lasso_fit) |> filter(estimate == 0) |> nrow()

[1] 29


The sex × waist interaction buys a small AUC gain — the simulated truth really does have sex-specific waist cut-offs, and a GLM cannot see them unless someone writes the term down. Tomorrow’s trees find it unaided.

title: Tutorial 1 · The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow, baseline
text:
Debrief (12.45)

You imputed BMI with the training median. A new patient arrives next year with no BMI. What value is used, and where did it come from?
Someone imputes before splitting, then splits. Which direction does their test AUC move, and why?
accuracy for your model is about 0.89. Explain to a clinician in one sentence why that number is meaningless here.







Debrief answers






The training median, stored inside the prepped recipe inside the fitted workflow. It travels with the model — that is what makes a workflow deployable.
Upwards (optimistic): the test rows’ imputed values were computed using test rows, so information crossed the split. Small here; large when missingness is heavy or the imputation model is flexible.
“Eighty-eight percent of people do not have it, so a model that says no to everyone is 88 % accurate and finds nobody.”

title: Tutorial 1 · The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow, baseline
text:
What to remember

Clean the codes before anything else: -9 is not a number; 3 is not Indian until you say so.
Event level first: levels(outcome)[1] == "Yes".
Split with strata; never look at the test set again until the very end.
A recipe is a plan; the workflow preps it on training data only, inside every fold.
If the AUC is too good, you leaked. Ask: could I know this predictor before the outcome?

# WHERE WE ARE ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5 folds, the recipe (impute -> dummy -> zero-variance -> normalise), a workflow, and the logistic baseline.
