title: Tutorial 2 · Decision trees and random forests
text:
1 · One decision tree






In one paragraph



A classification tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions. At each node it tries every predictor and every cut-point, and keeps the split that makes the two child nodes purest — lowest Gini impurity \(1 - \sum_k p_k^2\) (0 = all one class, 0.5 = a coin toss). It repeats inside each child until a stopping rule fires. A leaf’s prediction is the proportion of Yes among the training people who landed there. Continuous predictors are split at thresholds (BMI ≥ 27.5), which is why trees find cut-offs that nobody told them about — and why a tree’s prediction surface is a staircase, never a slope.


Trees do not need dummy variables or scaling, so a leaner recipe keeps the splits readable:

tree_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())


A small, pruned tree

tree_small <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0.005, tree_depth = 4, min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_small_fit <- workflow(tree_rec, tree_small) |> fit(dm_train)
tree_small_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE, extra = 104, type = 2)








Read it like a clinical algorithm: the root split is the single most informative question; each leaf shows the probability of Yes and the share of people who end up there.








Lever
decision_tree() argument
Effect




minimum people in a node before it may split
min_n
larger → simpler


maximum depth
tree_depth
smaller → simpler


cost-complexity pruning: a split must improve impurity by at least α
cost_complexity
larger → fewer leaves (CART’s cp)





An unconstrained tree — the overfitting signature

tree_big <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, tree_depth = 30, min_n = 2) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")
tree_big_fit <- workflow(tree_rec, tree_big) |> fit(dm_train)

bind_rows(
  small_train = augment(tree_small_fit, dm_train) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  small_test  = augment(tree_small_fit, dm_test)  |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  big_train   = augment(tree_big_fit,   dm_train) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  big_test    = augment(tree_big_fit,   dm_test)  |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  .id = "model"
)


  



The big tree is near-perfect on the data it was grown on and worse than the small tree on new data. It memorised noise: somewhere in it is a leaf that says “age < 23.5 and waist > 101 → Yes” because one person happened to fit. Everything that follows in this workshop is a way of growing trees without memorising.






Warning



We peeked at dm_test to make the overfitting point vivid. That is the last time until Tutorial 5. From here on, honest estimates come from the five folds of the training set.

title: Tutorial 2 · Decision trees and random forests
section: 2 · Random forest: many noisy trees, averaged
text:
2 · Random forest: many noisy trees, averaged






In one paragraph



Bagging: draw a bootstrap sample of the training rows, grow a full unpruned tree, repeat 500 times, and predict by voting. Each tree is a noisy, high-variance estimate; averaging many of them cancels the noise without adding bias — provided the trees differ. The random forest twist makes sure they do: at every split, a tree may only consider a random subset of mtry predictors, so the trees do not all put age at the root and become near-copies of each other. The rows left out of each bootstrap sample (about a third) are out-of-bag and give every tree a free validation set; the forest’s OOB error is an honest estimate you get without cross-validation.



rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 6, min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation", seed = 2026) |>
  set_mode("classification")

rf_wf <- workflow(tree_rec, rf_spec)










Knob
Meaning
Heuristic
Bias–variance




mtry
predictors tried at each split
√p for classification (here ~5–6)
higher → trees more alike; lower bias, more correlation


trees
number of trees
500–1000; more never hurts, only costs time
more → lower variance, until it plateaus


min_n
smallest node that may be split
5–10; larger smooths the probabilities
higher → simpler trees, more bias, less variance




Honest estimate: 5-fold cross-validation on the training set

set.seed(2026)
rf_res <- fit_resamples(rf_wf, resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics,
                        control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))
collect_metrics(rf_res)


  



Mean and standard error across five folds. The standard error is the number most papers forget to report — and the one that tells you whether two models actually differ.


Fit once on all the training data, and look inside

rf_fit <- fit(rf_wf, dm_train)
rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine()      # note "OOB prediction error (Brier s.)" - a free validation estimate

Ranger result

Call:
 ranger::ranger(x = maybe_data_frame(x), y = y, mtry = min_cols(~6,      x), num.trees = 500, min.node.size = min_rows(~10, x), importance = "permutation",      seed = 2026, num.threads = 1, verbose = FALSE, probability = TRUE) 

Type:                             Probability estimation 
Number of trees:                  500 
Sample size:                      3999 
Number of independent variables:  29 
Mtry:                             6 
Target node size:                 10 
Variable importance mode:         permutation 
Splitrule:                        gini 
OOB prediction error (Brier s.):  0.07834099 



rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> ranger::importance() |>     # the permutation importances ranger computed on the OOB rows
  tibble::enframe(name = "variable", value = "importance") |>   # tibble is not attached by tidymodels any more, hence the ::
  slice_max(importance, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(importance, reorder(variable, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0b4f6c") +
  labs(x = "permutation importance (rise in OOB error when the column is shuffled)", y = NULL,
       title = "Random forest: permutation importance") +
  theme_minimal()








Importance tells you which variables the forest leans on, not how (direction, shape, thresholds). Two caveats: impurity-based importance is biased toward continuous and many-level predictors (we used permutation importance, which is fairer); and correlated predictors share credit — bmi, waist, weight and bmi_cat each look less important than “adiposity” really is. Tutorial 6 adds partial dependence and SHAP for the how.


Compared with this morning’s baseline

lr_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm"))
set.seed(2026)
lr_res <- fit_resamples(lr_wf, dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics)

bind_rows(logistic = collect_metrics(lr_res), random_forest = collect_metrics(rf_res), .id = "model") |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "pr_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = model, colour = model)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = mean - std_err, xmax = mean + std_err), show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ .metric, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "5-fold CV estimate (± 1 SE)", y = NULL, title = "Same folds, same recipe idea, two model families")








Look at the error bars before declaring a winner. On tabular survey data a well-built logistic regression is hard to beat; the forest earns its extra AUC where the truth has interactions and thresholds (and here it does — the simulator planted several).

  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)

A1. Did any of your settings beat the heuristic by more than one standard error? A2. Which took longest (watch the verbose output)? Was the time worth it?








Solution A






forests <- list(
  heuristic = rand_forest(mtry = 6,  trees = 500,  min_n = 10) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  wide      = rand_forest(mtry = 15, trees = 500,  min_n = 10) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  deep      = rand_forest(mtry = 6,  trees = 500,  min_n = 2)  |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  smooth    = rand_forest(mtry = 4,  trees = 1000, min_n = 40) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification")
)
set.seed(2026)
forest_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(tree = tree_rec), models = forests) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)

rank_results(forest_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)


  



Typically everything lands within ~0.01 AUC and within one standard error. Random forests are famously forgiving — which is their great virtue and why tomorrow’s tuning session concentrates on XGBoost instead. Larger min_n usually improves the Brier score (smoother, better-calibrated probabilities) even when AUC is flat. Doubling trees roughly doubles the time and buys almost nothing beyond 500 here.









Task B · Does the forest see the same world as the GLM? (10 min)



Compare the top-10 permutation importances from rf_fit with the top-10 odds ratios (by |z|) from the logistic model in Tutorial 1. Where do they agree? Where do they differ, and can you explain the difference from how the two models work?








Solution B






lr_fit <- fit(lr_wf, dm_train)
tidy(lr_fit) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> arrange(desc(abs(statistic))) |> select(term, estimate, statistic) |> head(10)


  


rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> ranger::importance() |> tibble::enframe("variable", "importance") |> arrange(desc(importance)) |> head(10)


  



Both put age, family history, BMI/waist and ethnicity at the top. Differences: the GLM spreads ethnic over four dummy coefficients while the forest scores the factor once; the forest gives waist and bmi both high importance (it uses either interchangeably), the GLM concentrates the effect on one of them and leaves the other small; and interaction-only effects (family history × obesity) show up in the forest’s importances but cannot appear in a GLM without an interaction term.









Task C · Stretch




The OOB Brier score printed by ranger vs the 5-fold CV Brier from collect_metrics(rf_res): how close are they? Why would you still cross-validate?
Refit rf_spec with set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity"), pull ranger::importance() again and compare the ranking to the permutation version. Which variables move, and why? (Hint: think about how many distinct values each has.)









Solution C






They are usually within a few thousandths. OOB is free and honest for the forest itself, but it cannot evaluate the pre-processing (imputation, dummies) because those were estimated on all training rows, and it cannot compare the forest with models that have no OOB concept. Cross-validation evaluates the whole workflow.
Impurity importance inflates continuous variables with many split points (hh_income, waist, age) and deflates binary ones (fam_hx_dm, sex), because a variable with more candidate cut-points has more chances to reduce impurity by luck. Permutation importance does not have this bias — prefer it.

title: Tutorial 4 · Gradient boosting with XGBoost — and the bake-off
text:
1 · Boosting in one paragraph






Note



A random forest grows deep trees in parallel and averages them. Boosting grows shallow trees in sequence, each one fitted to what the ensemble so far gets wrong. Start with a trivial prediction (the log-odds of the prevalence). Compute, for every person, how wrong and in which direction — for classification that is the gradient of the log-loss, which for each person is simply observed − predicted probability. Fit a small tree to those residuals. Add it to the ensemble, shrunk by a learning rate. Repeat for hundreds of rounds. Each new tree is a step downhill on the loss function — gradient descent in the space of trees — which is the same idea that trains neural networks this afternoon. XGBoost is gradient boosting with serious engineering: a regularised objective (λ on leaf weights, γ to prune splits that do not pay for themselves), split finding on quantile sketches, a learned default direction for missing values, row and column subsampling, and multithreading.

2 · “Just use the defaults” vs a gentle setting

xgb_default <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.3, tree_depth = 6) |>      # xgboost's own defaults
  set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")

  set_engine("xgboost", counts = FALSE) |> set_mode("classification")

collect_metrics(xgb_two) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)

4 · XGBoost handles missing values itself
Every split learns a default direction for rows where the splitting variable is NA. So XGBoost can take the data without imputation — occasionally a better choice, because “missing” is then free to carry information (people who skipped the weight question may differ from those who did not).

rec_native_na <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>    # NA in a factor becomes NA in every dummy column - xgboost copes
  step_zv(all_predictors())

set.seed(2026)
xgb_na <- workflow_set(preproc = list(imputed = dm_rec, native_na = rec_native_na), models = list(xgb = xgb_gentle)) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)
collect_metrics(xgb_na) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)


  



Within noise here (7 % MAR missingness). Keep imputation when the same recipe must also serve a GLM, an SVM or a network — they cannot cope with NA.

Your turn (15 min)






Task A · The five-minute XGBoost



Three settings of your own against xgb_gentle, on the folds (never on the test set). Think about learning rate × trees first.

boosters <- list(
  gentle  = xgb_gentle,
  model_1 = boost_tree(trees = ___, learn_rate = ___, tree_depth = ___, min_n = ___) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  model_2 = boost_tree(trees = ___, learn_rate = ___, tree_depth = ___, min_n = ___) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  model_3 = boost_tree(trees = ___, learn_rate = ___, tree_depth = ___, min_n = ___) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
)
set.seed(2026)
boost_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = boosters) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026, verbose = TRUE)

  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)

A1. Did anyone beat gentle by more than one SE? A2. Did the deepest / fastest-learning setting win or lose?








Solution A






boosters <- list(
  gentle   = xgb_gentle,
  slow_deep = boost_tree(trees = 1000, learn_rate = 0.01, tree_depth = 6, min_n = 10) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  stumps    = boost_tree(trees = 1000, learn_rate = 0.05, tree_depth = 1, min_n = 20) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  fast      = boost_tree(trees = 200,  learn_rate = 0.3,  tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
)
set.seed(2026)
boost_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = boosters) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)
rank_results(boost_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)


  



stumps (depth-1 trees = an additive model) usually does surprisingly well — most of the signal is additive — but loses a little to depth 2–3, which can express the family-history × BMI interaction. fast overfits. Slow and deep is not better than gentle and costs four times the time.









Task B · Monotone constraints (stretch)



Biology says risk should never decrease with age in this range. Force it: set_engine("xgboost", monotone_constraints = ...) needs a vector with one entry per predictor column after the recipe (1 = increasing, 0 = free). Build it from dm_rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) column names, resample, and compare. (The warning about the sign being relative to the event level is expected — read it.)








Solution B






pred_names <- dm_rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> select(-undx_dm) |> names()
mono <- as.integer(pred_names == "age")      # one entry per predictor column, in recipe order: +1 for age, 0 for the rest

# NB: splice the vector in with !!mono. Resampling runs on parallel workers, and they do not have `mono`
# in scope - set_engine() would otherwise just store the *name* `mono` and each worker fails with
# "object 'mono' not found". !!mono embeds the actual integer vector in the spec.
xgb_mono <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.03, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", monotone_constraints = !!mono) |> set_mode("classification")

set.seed(2026)
mono_res <- fit_resamples(workflow(dm_rec, xgb_mono), dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics)
collect_metrics(mono_res) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class"))


  



Performance is essentially unchanged (the data already obey the constraint except at the very oldest ages, where the simulated risk falls slightly — survivorship), but the model is now guaranteed to behave sensibly on extrapolation, which is worth a lot when a clinician looks at a partial-dependence plot.

What to remember

Boosting = sequential error-correction; XGBoost = boosting plus regularisation and engineering.
Learning rate and number of trees trade off; fix one, let early stopping or CV choose the other.
Much more sensitive to settings than a forest — the reason Tutorial 5 exists.
workflow_set() + workflow_map() is how you compare families without copy-paste and without cheating.
When models tie within one SE, choose on calibration, interpretability, speed and deployability.

What you will do

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
text:
0 · Start

# WHERE WE ARE ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pipeline (T1), three families (T2-T4), tuning (T5). From here on the model is fixed: the tuned XGBoost from T5
# (loaded below from outputs/, with a fallback so this page also stands alone). NEW TODAY: judging it the way a
# clinician needs - confusion matrix at the real prevalence, ROC vs PR, calibration, choosing a threshold on
# purpose, class imbalance - and explaining it (importance, partial dependence, SHAP).
source("R/prep_nhms.R")
library(probably)      # calibration, thresholds
library(themis)        # class-imbalance recipe steps
library(DALEXtra)      # model-agnostic explanations for tidymodels
library(shapviz)       # SHAP plots
library(patchwork)
library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1))
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)

# the tuned XGBoost from Tutorial 5 (falls back to a fixed sensible version so this page stands alone)
if (file.exists("outputs/t05_xgb_last.rds")) {
  xgb_last <- readRDS("outputs/t05_xgb_last.rds")
} else {
  xgb_spec <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.03, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20, sample_size = 0.8) |>
    set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
  set.seed(2026)
  xgb_last <- last_fit(workflow(dm_rec, xgb_spec), dm_split, metrics = cls_metrics)
}
xgb_fit      <- extract_workflow(xgb_last)                       # fitted workflow (recipe + model)
xgb_final_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, extract_spec_parsnip(xgb_fit))  # same spec, unfitted, for resampling
test_preds   <- collect_predictions(xgb_last)                    # predictions on the locked test set

# out-of-fold predictions on the TRAINING set: every DECISION (threshold, calibration) is made on these,
# so the test set stays an honest final exam
set.seed(2026)
xgb_cv   <- fit_resamples(xgb_final_wf, dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))
cv_preds <- collect_predictions(xgb_cv)

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
section: 1 · A model is a probability; a decision is a threshold
text:
1 · A model is a probability; a decision is a threshold

test_preds |> select(undx_dm, .pred_Yes, .pred_class) |> head()


  



Every classifier we built outputs P(Yes); .pred_class is just P(Yes) ≥ 0.5. The 0.5 is a software default that silently assumes a false positive and a false negative cost the same. In screening they never do. So we evaluate the probabilities (discrimination, calibration) and the decision (confusion matrix at the threshold we will actually use) — separately.

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
section: 2 · The confusion matrix at the default threshold — and why it misleads
text:
2 · The confusion matrix at the default threshold — and why it misleads

test_preds |> conf_mat(undx_dm, .pred_class) |> autoplot(type = "heatmap")







test_preds |> conf_mat(undx_dm, .pred_class) |> summary() |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("accuracy", "sens", "spec", "ppv", "npv", "j_index"))


  



Accuracy near 0.89 looks fine and is worthless: 88 % of people are No. Sensitivity at 0.5 is poor. Nobody told the model that missing a diabetic costs more than an extra blood test.








Metric
Also called
Asks




sensitivity
recall, TPR
of the people who have it, how many did we flag?


specificity
TNR
of the people who don’t, how many did we leave alone?


PPV
precision
of the people we flagged, how many have it?


NPV
—
of the people we cleared, how many are truly clear?


J (Youden)
—
sens + spec − 1




PPV is not a property of the model

ppv_at <- function(sens, spec, prev) (sens * prev) / (sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev))
tibble(prevalence = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.116, 0.25)) |> mutate(ppv = ppv_at(sens = 0.80, spec = 0.75, prev = prevalence))


  



Same sensitivity and specificity, four populations, four PPVs. A model validated in a clinic (25 %) and deployed at a pasar malam (4 %) will see its PPV collapse. Report the prevalence you validated at — TRIPOD+AI asks for exactly this.

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
text:
3 · Threshold-free: ROC, precision–recall, gain

roc_auc(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes); pr_auc(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes)


  




  


p_roc  <- roc_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes)  |> autoplot() + labs(title = "ROC")
p_pr   <- pr_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes)   |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Precision-recall (baseline = 0.116)")
p_gain <- gain_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Gain: screen the top x%, find y% of cases")
p_roc + p_pr + p_gain









ROC is prevalence-blind — good for comparing models across populations, flattering on rare outcomes.
Precision–recall shows what the positive predictions are worth; its baseline is the prevalence.
Gain is the one for a programme manager: “if we can only test 20 % of adults, which 20 %, and what share of cases do we catch?”

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
section: 4 · Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say?
text:
4 · Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say?

brier_class(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes)    # 0 = perfect; predicting the prevalence for everyone gives ~0.10


  


cal_plot_breaks(test_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes, num_breaks = 10) + labs(title = "Reliability diagram, test set")







cal_plot_windowed(test_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes) + labs(title = "Windowed calibration, test set")








A point at (0.40, 0.25) means: when the model says 40 %, only 25 % actually have it. A model can have AUC 0.86 and still be badly calibrated — boosted trees and forests routinely are, and SMOTE’d models always are. A probability a clinician will show to a patient must be calibrated; a score that only sorts a queue cares less.

Fix it honestly: estimate on CV predictions, validate within resamples

cal_val <- cal_validate_logistic(xgb_cv, smooth = FALSE, metrics = metric_set(brier_class, roc_auc), save_pred = TRUE)   # smooth = FALSE -> Platt (2 parameters)
collect_metrics(cal_val)                      # uncalibrated vs calibrated: Brier down, AUC unchanged


  


collect_predictions(cal_val) |>
  cal_plot_breaks(truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes, .by = .type) + labs(title = "Before vs after logistic recalibration (CV)")







calibrator     <- cal_estimate_logistic(cv_preds, truth = undx_dm, smooth = FALSE)   # fitted on out-of-fold predictions
test_preds_cal <- cal_apply(test_preds, calibrator)                  # applied to the test set
bind_rows(raw = brier_class(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes), calibrated = brier_class(test_preds_cal, undx_dm, .pred_Yes), .id = "probs")


  



Recalibration moves the probabilities, not the ranking: AUC is untouched, Brier improves, thresholds become meaningful. Platt/logistic (smooth = FALSE: two parameters, robust) for most cases; probably’s default (smooth = TRUE) fits a spline-based GAM and is more flexible; isotonic when you have lots of data and a strange shape.

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
text:
5 · Choosing a threshold on purpose






thr_cv <- threshold_perf(cv_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.60, by = 0.01))

thr_cv |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("sensitivity", "specificity", "j_index")) |>
  ggplot(aes(.threshold, .estimate, colour = .metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = "Sensitivity / specificity by threshold (CV predictions)", x = "threshold on P(Yes)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








A community screen wants sensitivity around 0.80 and accepts the extra blood tests. Find the threshold on the CV predictions, then report it on the test set:

thr_chosen <- thr_cv |> filter(.metric == "sensitivity", .estimate >= 0.80) |> slice_max(.threshold, n = 1) |> pull(.threshold)
thr_chosen

[1] 0.1

test_thr <- test_preds |>
  mutate(.pred_screen = make_two_class_pred(.pred_Yes, levels = levels(undx_dm), threshold = thr_chosen) |> as.factor())

test_thr |> conf_mat(undx_dm, .pred_screen) |> summary() |> filter(.metric %in% c("sens", "spec", "ppv", "npv"))


  


test_thr |> summarise(flagged_pct = mean(.pred_screen == "Yes"),
                      cases_found = sum(.pred_screen == "Yes" & undx_dm == "Yes") / sum(undx_dm == "Yes"),
                      number_needed_to_screen = 1 / mean(undx_dm[.pred_screen == "Yes"] == "Yes"))


  



“Test the X % the model flags and you find Y % of the undiagnosed cases; about Z people tested per case found.” That is a sentence a programme manager can act on.






Decision curve analysis (the clinician’s metric)






if (requireNamespace("dcurves", quietly = TRUE)) {
  dcurves::dca(undx_dm ~ .pred_Yes, data = test_preds |> mutate(undx_dm = undx_dm == "Yes"),
               thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.5, by = 0.01), label = list(.pred_Yes = "XGBoost")) |> plot(smooth = TRUE)
}








Net benefit at threshold t = (TP − FP × t/(1−t)) / n: the threshold is the exchange rate between a false and a true positive. A model is useful only where its curve sits above both “test everyone” and “test no one”.

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
text:
7 · Explaining the model: global

xgboost::xgb.importance(model = extract_fit_engine(xgb_fit)) |>   # Gain = share of the total loss reduction attributed to each column
  as_tibble() |>
  slice_max(Gain, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(Gain, reorder(Feature, Gain))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0b4f6c") +
  labs(x = "gain (share of total loss reduction)", y = NULL, title = "XGBoost gain importance (model-specific)") +
  theme_minimal()








Model-agnostic tools work for anything with a predict() — including this afternoon’s network:

explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  xgb_fit,
  data  = dm_train |> select(-undx_dm),
  y     = dm_train$undx_dm == "Yes",
  predict_function_target_column = "Yes",     # our event level; DALEX would otherwise take the 2nd column
  label = "XGBoost (tuned)", verbose = FALSE
)

set.seed(2026)
vi_perm <- model_parts(explainer, loss_function = DALEX::loss_one_minus_auc, B = 10, N = 1000)
plot(vi_perm, max_vars = 15) + labs(title = "Permutation importance: AUC lost when a column is shuffled")








Correlated predictors share credit (BMI, waist, weight, bmi_cat each look weaker than “adiposity” is).

pdp <- model_profile(explainer, variables = c("age", "bmi", "waist"), N = 500)
plot(pdp) + labs(title = "Partial dependence: average predicted P(Yes) as one variable moves")







pdp_sex <- model_profile(explainer, variables = "waist", groups = "sex", N = 500)
plot(pdp_sex) + labs(title = "Waist by sex: two different cut-offs")








Look for the structure the trees found: the BMI step near 27.5, the age plateau, two waist curves for two sexes. The last one is an interaction a logistic model never saw unless someone hand-coded sex-specific cut-offs.

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
text:
8 · Explaining the model: local (SHAP)






Note



A Shapley value (game theory, 1953) is a variable’s fair share of the difference between this person’s prediction and the average prediction, averaged over every order in which the variables could be “added”. The shares add up exactly to the prediction. Two ways to get them: TreeSHAP reads them exactly off a tree ensemble in well under a second (what we do here); KernelSHAP estimates them for any model from predictions alone (Tutorial 7 uses it on the neural network — same plots, slower estimator).
One mechanical point first. The model never saw sex or ethnic; it saw the baked matrix the recipe produced — imputed, dummy-coded, normalised. SHAP values therefore come out per dummy column (sex_Male, ethnic_Chinese, …). shapviz can add the pieces of each factor back together (collapse) so you read one value per original variable, and plot it against the original, un-normalised values (X).



# 1. the people to explain, and the matrix the model actually saw for them
set.seed(2026)
X_explain <- dm_train |> select(-undx_dm) |> slice_sample(n = 500)          # 500 people is plenty for the plots
rec_fit   <- extract_recipe(xgb_fit)                                        # the recipe as TRAINED inside the workflow
X_baked   <- bake(rec_fit, new_data = X_explain, all_predictors(), composition = "matrix")

# 2. which dummy columns came from which factor (recipes keeps the book) -> one SHAP value per original variable
dummy_step <- tidy(rec_fit) |> filter(type == "dummy") |> pull(number)
facs       <- tidy(rec_fit, number = dummy_step) |> pull(terms) |> unique()   # the original factor columns
# each factor -> the dummy columns it produced. bake() cleans the level names (25-29.9 -> X25.29.9), so match on
# the "<factor>_" prefix of the ACTUAL baked columns rather than on the raw level names.
collapse   <- setNames(lapply(facs, \(f) grep(paste0("^", f, "_"), colnames(X_baked), value = TRUE)), facs)
collapse   <- collapse[lengths(collapse) > 0]

# 3. TreeSHAP: exact Shapley values straight from the fitted trees
sv <- shapviz(extract_fit_engine(xgb_fit), X_pred = X_baked, X = X_explain, collapse = collapse)

sv_importance(sv, kind = "beeswarm", max_display = 15) + labs(title = "SHAP summary: each dot is one person")







sv_dependence(sv, v = "bmi", color_var = "fam_hx_dm") + labs(title = "BMI, coloured by family history")







sv_dependence(sv, v = "waist", color_var = "sex")      + labs(title = "Waist, coloured by sex")








One patient:

X_explain[1, c("age", "sex", "bmi", "waist", "fam_hx_dm", "ethnic")]


  


sv_waterfall(sv, row_id = 1) + labs(title = "Why this person scored what they scored")







predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = X_explain[1, ], type = "break_down") |> plot()














What explanations do not mean




Not causal. SHAP and PDP describe the fitted function. “BMI drives risk up after 27.5” is a statement about the model, not about biology.
Not unique. Correlated predictors swap credit between fits; check stability across resamples before you tell a story.
Not a safety certificate. Use explanations to audit: agreement with what you know → trust up; disagreement → either you learned something or the model is cheating. Find out which.

text:
Your turn (10 min)






Task A · Two use cases, two thresholds











Use case
Requirement
Why




Community screen
sensitivity ≥ 0.85
a missed case costs years of silent disease; a false alarm costs one blood test


Confirmatory pre-selection (limited lab budget)
specificity ≥ 0.90
we can only afford to test a few; they had better be real



Find both thresholds on cv_preds; report flagged %, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and number-needed-to-screen on the test set. Then write the community-screen result as one sentence for a district health officer.
A2. The model was validated at 11.6 % prevalence; the district’s true prevalence is 6 %. Which numbers change, and which way?








Solution A






thr <- threshold_perf(cv_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.80, by = 0.01))
thr_screen  <- thr |> filter(.metric == "sensitivity", .estimate >= 0.85) |> slice_max(.threshold) |> pull(.threshold)
thr_confirm <- thr |> filter(.metric == "specificity", .estimate >= 0.90) |> slice_min(.threshold) |> pull(.threshold)

report_at <- function(preds, threshold) {
  preds |>
    mutate(.pred_rule = make_two_class_pred(.pred_Yes, levels = levels(undx_dm), threshold = threshold) |> as.factor()) |>
    summarise(threshold = threshold,
              flagged_pct = mean(.pred_rule == "Yes"),
              sens = sum(.pred_rule == "Yes" & undx_dm == "Yes") / sum(undx_dm == "Yes"),
              spec = sum(.pred_rule == "No"  & undx_dm == "No")  / sum(undx_dm == "No"),
              ppv  = sum(.pred_rule == "Yes" & undx_dm == "Yes") / sum(.pred_rule == "Yes"),
              nns  = 1 / ppv)
}
bind_rows(screen = report_at(test_preds, thr_screen), confirm = report_at(test_preds, thr_confirm), .id = "use_case")


  


ppv_at(0.85, 0.65, 0.116); ppv_at(0.85, 0.65, 0.06)

[1] 0.2416667


[1] 0.1342105


A model sentence: “Testing the ~40 % of adults the model flags would find ~85 % of undiagnosed cases; about four people tested per case found.” A2: sensitivity and specificity are (roughly) properties of model + threshold and stay put; PPV falls (fewer true cases among the flagged), NPV rises, number-needed-to-screen rises; the flagged percentage also shifts because the score distribution changes with the population.









Task B · Does it work equally well for everyone?



Using collect_predictions(xgb_last) joined back to dm_test, compute AUC and sensitivity at thr_chosen by sex and by ethnic. Any group the model under-serves? What would you do about it?








Solution B






by_group <- test_preds |>
  bind_cols(dm_test |> select(sex, ethnic)) |>      # last_fit predictions are in test-set row order
  mutate(.pred_screen = make_two_class_pred(.pred_Yes, levels = levels(undx_dm), threshold = thr_chosen) |> as.factor())

by_group |> group_by(sex)    |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes)


  


by_group |> group_by(ethnic) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes)


  


by_group |> group_by(sex)    |> sensitivity(undx_dm, .pred_screen)


  



Small groups (Others, Other Bumiputera) have wide uncertainty; look at the SE before reading a difference. If one group is genuinely under-flagged at the shared threshold, options are group-specific thresholds, re-weighting, more data — and, always, saying so in the paper. fairmodels extends DALEX with the standard fairness metrics.

title: Tutorial 6 · Evaluation, calibration and explanation
text:
What to remember

Accuracy lies at 12 % prevalence. Report sens/spec/PPV/NPV at the threshold you will use, at the prevalence you face.
ROC to compare models; PR and gain for what the predictions are worth; Brier and a calibration plot for honesty.
Choose the threshold from the use case, on CV predictions; report it on the test set, in people.
SMOTE moves the threshold in disguise and breaks calibration. Move the threshold instead.
Importance → which; PDP → how; SHAP → why this person. None of it is causal.

text:
The data


data/nhms_synthetic.csv — 5,000 adults, 41 variables, NHMS-style.

Sociodemographics, lifestyle, anthropometry, family history
Clinic measurements: BP, random blood sugar, cholesterol
Three outcomes: undiagnosed diabetes / hypertension / high cholesterol

The question for both days: who has undiagnosed diabetes? Take-home challenge: who has undiagnosed hypertension?


It is synthetic. Simulated from plausible Malaysian risk gradients so that the models have something real to find — and so that, at the end of Day 2, we can open the simulator and check what they found. No row is a person. No number is an estimate of anything.
Why not real NHMS data? It is confidential, and the usual way of de-identifying it (scrambling each column) destroys the relationships between variables that a model has to learn.



Be upfront. Researchers respect it. Mention that the generator is in data-raw/ and we’ll reveal the “truth” at the end of Day 2 — motivates the explainability section.

title: Learning how the machine learns
section: A model is a function fitted to data
text:
A model is a function fitted to data
\[\hat{y} = f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p)\]

Logistic regression: \(f\) is a sigmoid of a weighted sum. You fit it by maximum likelihood.
A random forest: \(f\) is an average of 500 decision trees. You fit it by greedy splitting.
A neural network: \(f\) is a stack of weighted sums and squashes. You fit it by gradient descent.


Statistics and machine learning are the same activity with different priorities. ML optimises predictive accuracy on new data and lets the data choose the shape of \(f\). Classical modelling optimises interpretable, unbiased estimates of effects and chooses the shape of \(f\) by hand.


Breiman’s “Two Cultures” (2001). Shmueli “To explain or to predict?” (2010). This slide pre-empts the “it’s just logistic regression” objection by agreeing with it.

title: Learning how the machine learns
section: Explain or predict? Two different jobs
text:
Explain or predict? Two different jobs









Explanatory (classical epi)
Predictive (this workshop)




Question
Does smoking cause higher risk?
Who, in this population, has it now?


Hero statistic
Odds ratio with CI, p-value
AUC, calibration, sensitivity at a threshold


Variable selection
DAG, confounding, parsimony
Whatever is available before the outcome and improves prediction


Validation
Model assumptions, residuals
Performance on unseen data


Overfitting
A nuisance
The central enemy


Interactions, non-linearity
Added by hand, if theory says so
Learned from data




A predictor does not have to be causal to be useful. A causal effect does not have to predict well. Keep the two jobs apart in your head and in your paper.

title: Learning how the machine learns
text:
The supervised-learning contract



You have labelled examples: \((x_i, y_i)\) for \(i = 1 \dots n\).
You want a rule that maps new \(x\) → \(y\).
Classification: \(y\) is a category (undiagnosed DM: yes/no).
Regression: \(y\) is a number (HbA1c, length of stay).

The machine “learns” by adjusting the rule until it is wrong as rarely as possible on examples it has not seen.

Other kinds, not today:

Unsupervised: no \(y\) — clustering, dimension reduction (phenotypes, PCA).
Reinforcement: learn by reward (dosing policies; mostly research).
Generative / LLMs: learn to produce data; a story for another workshop.

text:
The lifecycle of a predictive model

Question — for whom, deciding what, with what information available at that moment?
Data — assemble, clean, audit for leakage
Split — lock away a test set
Pre-process — a recipe, estimated on training data only
Train — one or several model families
Validate — resampling, honest estimates with error bars
Tune — search hyperparameters, on resamples
Evaluate — on the test set, once; discrimination and calibration
Explain — importance, dependence, SHAP; sanity-check against domain knowledge
Decide — threshold, decision rule, report (TRIPOD+AI)
Deploy & monitor — drift, recalibration, fairness

Day 1 = steps 1–5. Day 2 = steps 6–10. Step 11 = the last slide tomorrow.

section: The curve that explains every hyperparameter
text:
The curve that explains every hyperparameter






High bias: the model is too simple to capture the signal — bad on training and test data.
High variance: the model memorised the training data’s noise — great on training, bad on test.
Every tuning knob you meet (tree depth, mtry, penalty, hidden units, cost, k) moves you along this x-axis.

title: Learning how the machine learns
text:
The one rule

Never evaluate a model on the data it was trained on.
Training error always goes down as the model gets more flexible. It tells you nothing about new patients. Every honest number in this workshop comes from data the model did not see: a held-out fold or the locked test set.

Corollaries you will see today:

A single train/test split is a noisy estimate → resample (Day 2, 9.15).
Anything estimated from data (imputation medians, scaling, SMOTE) must be estimated inside the training fold → recipes.
If it looks too good, it probably is: suspect leakage before celebrating.

title: Learning how the machine learns
text:
Why not just call xgboost()?
You can. Then ranger() wants a formula, xgboost() wants a matrix, kernlab wants scaled numerics, every package returns predict() output in a different shape, and the confusion-matrix code gets copy-pasted four times with four different bugs.


tidymodels gives you:

one way to split (rsample)
one way to pre-process (recipes)
one way to specify a model and swap the engine (parsnip)
one object that bundles both (workflows)
one way to resample & tune (tune, dials, finetune)
one way to measure (yardstick, probably)
one way to compare many (workflowsets)

title: Decision trees and random forests
text:
The parts of a tree






Classification tree: leaves hold a class and a proportion (→ a probability).
Regression tree: leaves hold a mean.

title: Decision trees and random forests
section: Which question goes at the top? Gini impurity
text:
Which question goes at the top? Gini impurity
\[\text{Gini}(\text{node}) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2 \qquad\text{(0 = pure; 0.5 = a coin toss for two classes)}\]
For each candidate split compute the weighted average Gini of the two children; the lowest wins. Repeat inside each child. Stop when nothing improves, or when a stopping rule says so.







Adapted from StatQuest (2019)

title: Decision trees and random forests
text:
Comparing candidates — and continuous predictors




For a continuous predictor: sort the values, take the midpoint between each adjacent pair as a candidate threshold, compute the Gini for each, keep the best.
That is why trees find cut-offs (BMI ≥ 27.5, waist ≥ 80 cm) nobody told them about — and why a tree’s prediction surface is a staircase, never a slope.
Entropy / information gain: same idea with a log instead of a square. It rarely matters which.

title: Decision trees and random forests
section: Growing until pure — and the problem with that
text:
Growing until pure — and the problem with that





The leaf “age < 12.5” holds one person. The tree is now confident about a sample of one. That is overfitting, in a picture.

Adapted from StatQuest (2019)

text:
Keeping a tree honest








Lever
decision_tree()
Effect




minimum people in a node before it may split
min_n
larger → simpler


maximum depth
tree_depth
smaller → simpler


cost-complexity pruning: a split must improve impurity by ≥ α
cost_complexity
larger → fewer leaves (CART’s cp)




decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0.005, tree_depth = 4, min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

Regression trees work identically with the sum of squared residuals in place of Gini.

title: Decision trees and random forests
text:
Single trees: the honest verdict


For

Reads like a clinical algorithm
Handles factors, skew and interactions with no pre-processing
Fast; missing values via surrogate splits (rpart)


Against

Unstable: change a few rows, get a different tree
Inaccurate: staircases approximate smooth truths badly
Overfits unless pruned; pruning is a guess



“Trees have one aspect that prevents them from being the ideal tool for predictive learning, namely inaccuracy.” — Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning
The fix: don’t grow one tree. Grow hundreds and combine them. Two ways to combine → two families: bagging (today) and boosting (tomorrow).

title: Decision trees and random forests
text:
Bagging: bootstrap + aggregate

Draw a bootstrap sample (n rows, with replacement) from the training data.
Grow a full, unpruned tree on it.
Repeat 500 times.
To predict: run the new person through all 500 trees and vote (classification) or average (regression).

Why it works: each tree is a noisy, high-variance estimate of the truth. Averaging many noisy estimates cancels the noise (variance ↓) without adding bias — provided the trees are different. Hence the bootstrap.
About a third of rows are left out of each bootstrap sample → out-of-bag (OOB) rows → a free validation set for every tree → the OOB error is an honest estimate you get without cross-validation.

title: Decision trees and random forests
text:
Random forests = bagging + a twist





The twist: at each split a tree may only consider a random subset of mtry predictors (default ≈ √p).
Without it every bootstrap tree would put the same dominant predictor (age) at the root and the trees would be highly correlated — and averaging correlated things does not reduce variance much. Random feature subsets decorrelate the trees.

Catalyst Earth (2023)

section: What a forest can tell you about the variables
text:
What a forest can tell you about the variables

Impurity importance (how much a variable reduced Gini, summed over all splits): fast; biased toward continuous and many-level predictors.
Permutation importance (shuffle a column in the OOB data; see how much error rises): slower; fairer; correlated predictors share credit (waist and BMI each look weaker than they are).


rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> ranger::importance() |> tibble::enframe("variable", "importance") |> arrange(desc(importance))

Importance says which. It does not say how (direction, shape) — that is tomorrow (PDP, SHAP).

title: Decision trees and random forests
section: Where forests win, and where they don’t
text:
Where forests win, and where they don’t
Win: tabular data with mixed types, interactions, thresholds; moderate n; little time to tune; a strong, honest baseline for almost any health prediction problem.
Don’t:

Extrapolation — a tree cannot predict outside the range it saw (a 110-year-old gets the 92-year-old’s leaf).
Smooth additive truths — a GLM with the right spline beats a staircase.
Calibration — forest probabilities are pulled toward the middle (few 0.05s, few 0.95s); recalibrate before showing them to a patient.
Raw signals (images, waveforms, text) — neural networks’ home turf.

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
text:
Fix the previous model’s mistakes






Start with a trivial prediction — the log-odds of the prevalence.
Compute, for every person, how wrong and in which direction.
Fit a small tree (depth 1–6) to those errors.
Add it to the ensemble, shrunk by a learning rate (0.01–0.3).
Repeat for hundreds of rounds.


Adapted from StatQuest (2019)

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
text:
Why “gradient”?





“How wrong, in which direction” is the gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction. For log-loss and a probability output that gradient is simply observed − predicted. Each new tree is a step downhill on the loss function; the learning rate is the step size. Gradient descent in the space of trees — the same idea trains neural networks this afternoon, with weights instead of trees.

Hikmat et al. (2021)

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
section: Learning rate and number of trees trade off
text:
Learning rate and number of trees trade off





Small steps + many trees: slow, smooth, lower minimum. Big steps: fast, then overshoots and overfits. Rule: fix a learning rate in 0.01–0.1, then let early stopping or cross-validation choose the number of trees. Do not tune both freely.

This is the StatQuest “XGBoost Part 2: Classification” example. We’ll build the first tree with real numbers.

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
section: Similarity score: how “pure” is a group of residuals?
text:
Similarity score: how “pure” is a group of residuals?
\[\text{Similarity}=\frac{\left(\sum \text{residual}\right)^2}{\sum p(1-p)+\lambda}\qquad(\lambda=0\text{ for now})\]
The denominator \(\sum p(1-p)\) is the Cover — how much information the group carries. At \(p=0.5\) each person adds \(0.25\).
Root (all four residuals): \[\text{Sim}=\frac{(-0.5+0.5+0.5-0.5)^2}{4(0.25)+0}=\frac{0}{1}=\mathbf{0}\]
Residuals that cancel → similarity 0 (a useless group). Residuals that are large and agree → high similarity. The tree’s job is to split the pile into agreeing groups.

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
section: Gain: is a split worth making?
text:
Gain: is a split worth making?
Split the lowest dose (the first No) off from the other three:




residuals
\(\sum p(1-p)\)
Similarity




Left leaf
−0.5
0.25
\((-0.5)^2/0.25=\mathbf{1.00}\)


Right leaf
+0.5, +0.5, −0.5
0.75
\((0.5)^2/0.75=\mathbf{0.33}\)



\[\text{Gain}=\text{Sim}_{\text{left}}+\text{Sim}_{\text{right}}-\text{Sim}_{\text{root}}=1.00+0.33-0=\mathbf{1.33}\]
XGBoost tries every threshold and keeps the biggest Gain — this is what replaces Gini.

Cover check: min_child_weight (default 1) is the smallest Cover a leaf may have. At p≈0.5 that’s ~4 people — so on a toy this small you’d lower it; on real data it just means “no micro-leaves.”

λ shrinks every similarity → shrinks the Gain → fewer splits look worthwhile, and (next slide) the steps get smaller. λ = “don’t trust small groups.”

γ (gamma): prune the weak splits
Rule: keep a split only if Gain > γ. (Equivalently, prune if \(\text{Gain}-\gamma<0\).)

γ is your “minimum worthwhile improvement.” Bigger γ → simpler tree. In tidymodels it’s loss_reduction.

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
section: Output value, then η (eta): take the step
text:
Output value, then η (eta): take the step
The leaf’s output uses the same numerator, but not squared: \[\text{Output}=\frac{\sum \text{residual}}{\sum p(1-p)+\lambda}\;\Rightarrow\; \text{Left}=\frac{-0.5}{0.25}=\mathbf{-2.0},\quad \text{Right}=\frac{0.5}{0.75}=\mathbf{+0.67}\]
Update each person, shrunk by the learning rate η = 0.3: \(\;\log(\text{odds})_{\text{new}}=\log(\text{odds})_{\text{old}}+\eta\cdot\text{Output}\), then \(p=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\log(\text{odds})}}\).








Leaf

\(0+0.3(-2.0)=-0.6\)
\(1/(1+e^{0.6})=\mathbf{0.35}\) — pushed toward No


Right (mostly Yes)
\(0+0.3(0.67)=+0.20\)
\(1/(1+e^{-0.2})=\mathbf{0.55}\) — nudged toward Yes



Now recompute residuals from these new probabilities, grow the next tree, repeat hundreds of times.

title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
section: Regularisation in one slide (needed again at 14.00)
text:
Regularisation in one slide (needed again at 14.00)

L2 (ridge, λ, “penalty”): shrink all weights toward zero; none become exactly zero. Smoother, more stable.
L1 (lasso, “mixture = 1”): shrink and zero out some weights — built-in variable selection.
Toy-box analogy: L1 lets only a fixed number of toys in; L2 lets all of them in but packs them loosely.

Where you meet it: glmnet (penalty, mixture); XGBoost (λ, γ, loss_reduction); SVM (cost is 1/λ); neural networks (weight decay).
Regularisation = a deliberate bit of bias bought with a large drop in variance.

title: Evaluation and explainability
section: A model is a probability. A decision is a threshold.
text:
A model is a probability. A decision is a threshold.

augment(xgb_fit, dm_test) |> select(undx_dm, .pred_Yes, .pred_class)
#>   undx_dm .pred_Yes .pred_class
#>   No          0.07  No
#>   Yes         0.41  No          <- a "miss" at threshold 0.5; a "hit" at 0.3


Every classifier we built outputs P(Yes). .pred_class is just P(Yes) ≥ 0.5.
0.5 is a software default. It encodes the belief that a false positive and a false negative cost the same. In screening they never do.
So: evaluate the probabilities (discrimination, calibration) and the decision (confusion matrix at the threshold you will actually use).

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Accuracy at 11.6 % prevalence
A model that says “No” to everyone has accuracy 0.884, sensitivity 0, and finds nobody.
Our honest logistic model at threshold 0.5: accuracy ≈ 0.89, sensitivity ≈ 0.2. It is barely better than the useless model on accuracy and vastly better on what matters.

Never lead with accuracy for an imbalanced outcome. Lead with sensitivity and specificity at the operating threshold, PPV/NPV at the prevalence you validated in, and AUC with a CI.

title: Evaluation and explainability
section: PPV is not a property of the model
text:
PPV is not a property of the model





\[\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{sens} \times \text{prev}}{\text{sens} \times \text{prev} + (1-\text{spec})(1-\text{prev})}\]
Validate in a clinic at 25 % prevalence, deploy at a pasar malam at 4 %, and the same model’s PPV falls by two thirds. Report the prevalence. Recompute PPV for the deployment population.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
ROC and AUC






ROC: sensitivity vs 1−specificity at every threshold. AUC = P(a random case scores higher than a random non-case). 0.5 = coin; 1 = perfect.
Prevalence-blind — good for comparing models across populations; flattering on rare outcomes, because false positives are a small fraction of a huge negative class.
Precision–recall: PPV vs sensitivity. Baseline is the prevalence. Shows what the flagged people are worth. Use it alongside ROC when the outcome is rare.

title: Evaluation and explainability
section: Gain and lift: for the programme manager
text:
Gain and lift: for the programme manager

gain_curve(test_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> autoplot()


x: fraction of the population you screen, ranked by model score; y: fraction of all cases you capture.
“If we can only test 20 % of adults, the top-scoring 20 % contains 55 % of the undiagnosed cases” — that is a sentence a budget holder understands.
Lift = gain ÷ fraction screened: 55 % / 20 % = 2.75× better than testing at random.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Brier score
\[\text{Brier} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (p_i - y_i)^2 \qquad\text{(0 = perfect, lower is better)}\]

The mean squared error of the probabilities. Rewards being right and being honest about uncertainty.
Decomposes into calibration (are the probabilities right on average?) + refinement/discrimination (are they spread out usefully?).
Reference points: predicting the prevalence for everyone gives prev × (1 − prev) ≈ 0.10 here. A model needs to beat that.
brier_class() in yardstick; include it in every metric_set().

title: Evaluation and explainability
section: Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say?
text:
Calibration: do the probabilities mean what they say?




A reliability diagram bins people by predicted probability and plots the observed event rate per bin.

On the diagonal: “40 %” means 40 %.
Above: under-confident. Below: over-confident.
A model can have AUC 0.86 and still be badly calibrated — random forests and boosted trees routinely are; SMOTE’d models always are.


cal_plot_breaks(test_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes)
cal_plot_windowed(test_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_Yes)

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Fixing calibration honestly

cal_val <- cal_validate_logistic(xgb_cv, smooth = FALSE, metrics = metric_set(brier_class, roc_auc))
collect_metrics(cal_val)          # uncalibrated vs calibrated, estimated WITHIN resamples

calibrator     <- cal_estimate_logistic(cv_preds, truth = undx_dm, smooth = FALSE)   # fitted on CV predictions (Platt)
test_preds_cal <- cal_apply(test_preds, calibrator)                  # applied to the test set


Platt / logistic recalibration: fit truth ~ logit(p); two parameters; robust (smooth = FALSE; probably’s default smooth = TRUE is a GAM). Isotonic: monotone step function; flexible, needs more data. Beta calibration in between.
Fit the calibrator on out-of-fold predictions, never on the test set.
Recalibration changes the probabilities, not the ranking → AUC unchanged, Brier improves, thresholds become meaningful.
Clinical probabilities that will be shown to people (risk of 23 %) must be calibrated. Rankings that only sort a queue care less.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Choosing the threshold on purpose






thr <- threshold_perf(cv_preds, undx_dm, .pred_Yes, thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.6, 0.01))









Approach
Rule
Comment




Target sensitivity
smallest threshold with sens ≥ 0.80
screening programmes


Target specificity
threshold with spec ≥ 0.90
expensive confirmatory tests


Capacity
threshold that flags exactly the x % you can test
the take-home challenge


Youden’s J
maximise sens + spec − 1
assumes equal costs; rarely true


Cost-weighted
minimise FN × cost_FN + FP × cost_FP
best when you can name the costs



Decide on CV predictions. Report on the test set. Then write it in people: “test 35 %, find 80 %, 5 tests per case”.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Decision curve analysis (the clinician’s metric)

dcurves::dca(undx_dm ~ .pred_Yes, data = test_preds |> mutate(undx_dm = undx_dm == "Yes"),
             thresholds = seq(0.02, 0.5, 0.01)) |> plot(smooth = TRUE)


Net benefit at threshold t = (TP − FP × t/(1−t)) / n. The threshold is the exchange rate between a false positive and a true positive.
Compare the model to test everyone and test no one across plausible thresholds. A model is useful only where its curve sits above both.
Vickers & Elkin (2006); now expected in clinical prediction papers alongside AUC and calibration.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Class imbalance: the honest version






Up-sampling, down-sampling, SMOTE (themis) make the training set 50/50. The model then thinks prevalence is 50 % → every probability inflates → sensitivity at 0.5 rises. That is a threshold change in disguise, with calibration destroyed as a side effect. AUC barely moves.
Preferred: keep the real data, pick the threshold you need, recalibrate if required. Use class weights (case_weights, xgboost scale_pos_weight) if the algorithm needs help ranking the rare class.
SMOTE belongs in the last resort drawer, with a calibration step after it.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Why explain?



Trust: is it predicting for the right reasons, or did it learn the hospital ID?
Debugging: leakage shows up as one absurdly dominant variable.
Science: hypothesis generation (that sex-specific waist threshold).
Regulation & ethics: patients and clinicians are entitled to a reason; some jurisdictions require it.
Fairness: does it work equally well by sex and ethnicity?

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
The taxonomy









Global (the whole model)
Local (one person)




Model-specific
coefficients (GLM), gain importance (xgboost), impurity importance (RF)
tree path (single tree)


Model-agnostic (works for anything, incl. the neural net)
permutation importance, partial dependence (PDP), ALE, SHAP summary
SHAP waterfall / force, break-down, LIME, ICE



Tools today: the engines’ own importances (ranger::importance(), xgboost::xgb.importance()), DALEX/DALEXtra (permutation importance, PDP, break-down), shapviz (TreeSHAP today; kernelshap for any model, tomorrow’s network).

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Which variables matter: importance

xgboost::xgb.importance(model = extract_fit_engine(xgb_fit))               # model-specific (gain, cover, frequency)

explainer <- explain_tidymodels(xgb_fit, data = dm_train |> select(-undx_dm),
                                y = dm_train$undx_dm == "Yes", predict_function_target_column = "Yes")
model_parts(explainer, loss_function = loss_one_minus_auc, B = 10) |> plot()   # permutation importance


Permutation importance: shuffle one column, measure how much AUC falls. Model-agnostic and honest about predictive value.
Caveats: correlated predictors share credit (BMI, waist, weight, bmi_cat all look weaker than “adiposity” is); impurity importance is biased toward continuous/high-cardinality predictors; importance says nothing about direction.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
How risk moves: partial dependence

model_profile(explainer, variables = c("age", "bmi", "waist"), N = 500) |> plot()
model_profile(explainer, variables = "waist", groups = "sex", N = 500) |> plot()    # interaction check


PDP: set age = 50 for everyone, predict, average; repeat for every age. The curve is the model’s average response to that variable.
ICE curves: the same per person — shows heterogeneity hidden by the average. ALE plots fix the PDP’s problem with correlated predictors (it asks the model about impossible people, e.g. BMI 15 with waist 120).
Look for the structure the trees found: the BMI step near 27.5, the age plateau, two waist curves for two sexes.

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
Why this person: SHAP



Shapley value (game theory, 1953): a variable’s fair share of the difference between this prediction and the average prediction, averaged over every order in which variables could be “added”.
Properties: the contributions add up exactly to the prediction; consistent; model-agnostic.


X_baked <- bake(extract_recipe(xgb_fit), X_explain, all_predictors(), composition = "matrix")
sv <- shapviz(extract_fit_engine(xgb_fit), X_pred = X_baked, X = X_explain, collapse = dummies)

sv_importance(sv, kind = "beeswarm")                 # global: importance AND direction
sv_dependence(sv, v = "bmi", color_var = "fam_hx_dm")  # shape + interaction
sv_waterfall(sv, row_id = 1)                         # local: this person


The model saw the baked matrix, so SHAP comes out per dummy column; collapse adds each factor back together.
TreeSHAP (exact, instant) for tree ensembles; KernelSHAP (kernelshap(), approximate, any model) for the neural net this afternoon — same plots.



Linberry (2021)

title: Evaluation and explainability
text:
What explanations do not mean

Not causal. SHAP/PDP describe the fitted function. “BMI drives risk up after 27.5” is a statement about the model. Whether BMI causes diabetes is a different study.
Not unique. Correlated predictors swap credit between fits; importance rankings shift across bootstrap resamples. Check stability before you tell a story.
Not the whole truth. A PDP averages away interactions; a beeswarm hides calibration; a waterfall for one person says nothing about the next.
Not a safety certificate. A model can be explainable and wrong, or unexplainable and right. Explanations are for auditing, not for absolving.


Use explanations to ask: does this agree with what we know? Agreement → trust up. Disagreement → either you learned something or the model is cheating. Find out which.

title: Evaluation and explainability
section: Fairness: check it, don’t assume it
text:
Fairness: check it, don’t assume it

collect_predictions(xgb_last) |>
  bind_cols(dm_test |> select(sex, ethnic)) |>

Predictors: when they were measured relative to the outcome; how missing data were handled at model development and at deployment
Sample size rationale (events per candidate predictor; pmsampsize)
Model development: resampling, tuning ranges and selection, software versions, seeds
Performance: discrimination with CI, calibration plot (not just slope/intercept), clinical utility (decision curve), by subgroup
Fairness and open code/data (or a reason why not)
Usability: how a user gets a prediction; what the threshold is and why

section: The reveal: what the simulator actually planted
text:
The reveal: what the simulator actually planted
The data were simulated (data-raw/simulate_nhms_synthetic.py). For undiagnosed diabetes the truth contains:

a steep age effect from 35 to 62, then a decline (survivorship)
a BMI threshold at 27.5 (the Asian obesity cut-off), stronger than the linear BMI slope
family history × obesity — the biggest single term
Indian ethnicity × overweight; central obesity × inactivity with sex-specific waist cut-offs (M ≥ 90, F ≥ 80 cm)
a young-obese bump (age < 35 and BMI ≥ 30); male smokers only; rural, poor and ≥ 50
and rbs generated from the outcome — the leak.

Did the SHAP dependence plots find the family-history × BMI bands? The two waist curves? Did logistic regression — which cannot see interactions unless told — keep up anyway? That gap between what the truth contains and what each family can express is the whole reason to run a bake-off.

title: Verdict, the reveal, and where next
text:
Two days in ten rules

Ask when every predictor is known. If it is known because of the outcome, it is out.
Event level first. levels(y)[1] == "Yes".
Split with strata; lock the test set. It answers one question, once.
Pre-process inside the recipe, so it is re-estimated inside every fold.
Resample everything. Report mean ± SE. One split is one draw.
Tune on resamples, with ranges you can defend; prefer the simplest model within one SE.
Accuracy lies at low prevalence. Sens/spec/PPV at the threshold you will use, at the prevalence you will face.
Probabilities must be calibrated before anyone acts on them. Brier + reliability plot, always.
Choose the threshold from the use case, on CV predictions. Write it in people.
Explain to audit, not to absolve. Importance → which; PDP → how; SHAP → why this person. None of it is causal.

           step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
zoo   <- workflow_set(list(rec), list(glm = ..., rf = ..., svm = ..., xgb = ..., nn = ...)) |> workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = folds)
tuned <- tune_race_anova(workflow(rec, winner_with_tune()), folds, grid = 20)
final <- last_fit(finalize_workflow(..., select_best(tuned, metric = "roc_auc")), split)
cal_plot_breaks(collect_predictions(final), y, .pred_Yes);  threshold_perf(cv_preds, y, .pred_Yes)
shapviz(extract_fit_engine(final), X_pred = baked_X, X = X, collapse = dummies) |> sv_importance("beeswarm")   # or kernelshap() for any model
